https://www.dw.com/en/sudan-civil-war-wh.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Hedr Hundreds of thousands of Sudanese have been displaced Image: Sarah Vuylsteke/NRC/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement Flattened houses and rubble where a school once stood: These are the scenes that have appeared in footage of the Sudanese city of el-Obeid published by Ayin Network, a nonpartisan Sudanese media outlet. Drone attacks by the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have caused enormous damage to civilian infrastructure, including power grids, transformers, water treatment plants, schools, universities and hospitals in the capital of North Kordofan. The local population is struggling to survive, according to Ahmed Awad, a native of el-Obeid and a project manager for children's rights organization Plan International there. The city — whose population previously numbered half a million but has now become home to several hundred thousand people who are displaced — is under siege, he added. There is a shortage of medical supplies as well as food and safe, clean water, and Awad said he saw long lines of people at just one water pump: "Sometimes you can spend all day to get one liter of water for two or three days." Most of the time, children and teenagers are the ones sent to fetch water. Millions across Sudan are going hungry, including over 825,000 children under 5 suffering from severe acute malnutrition Image: AFP He added that a drone had hit a primary school and killed three children, which had caused trauma among other children, many of whom no longer dared go to school. "One of the mothers said three of her children cannot sleep because they are always in fear of something happening again," he said. Even when they're sitting in their classrooms, they live with the constant fear that a drone could strike at any moment. Awad and his colleagues at Plan International are working to provide psychological support to the affected children. Sudan's strategic crossroads El-Obeid is a strategically important location. The city is a trading hub in the middle of the desert on the only major route between Sudan's capital, Khartoum — which is controlled by the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) — and the western Darfur region, large parts of which are under the control of the RSF. El-Obeid is currently controlled by the army, which has some 13,000 soldiers stationed there, and has been on the front line since fighting shifted from Darfur to Kordofan at the beginning of the year. The RSF has deployed troops to about 30 kilometers (18.6 miles) beyond the city limits, and has been using drones to bomb civilian infrastructure. Warnings of mass atrocities Analysts, aid organizations and the United Nations have warned that the RSF could soon capture el-Obeid. They fear a similar scenario to that which unfolded in the city of el-Fasher in the neighboring state of North Darfur in October 2025, when the RSF began by bombing infrastructure before storming the city after an 18-month siege. Earlier this year, a UN Fact-Finding Mission for the Sudan presented to the United Nations Human Rights Council in Geneva detailed atrocities in the capture of el-Fasher and identified "hallmarks of genocide." “We warn that an escalation of the situation could lead to a repeat of the horrific human rights violations and abuses against civilians that we documented in Al-Fashir,” numerous human rights organizations said in a joint appeal. "We are alarmed by the ongoing hostilities around the city, including frequent drone strikes," said Pekka Haavisto, the UN chief's personal envoy for Sudan , in June. "These are already affecting the civilians and disrupting humanitarian aid to the city. Any further escalation of the situation would place thousands of people at risk." Growing up under drones The situation is particularly dire for the children trapped in el-Obeid, says Francesco Lanino, deputy country director of the children's charity Save the Children in Sudan. Drone attacks on schools and displacement camps have caused severe trauma. Lanino recently visited the Tawila displacement camp near el-Fashir in Darfur, which was taken over by the RSF in October. There, he encountered children struggling to process what had happened to them. "We met several children who refused to speak afterwards," Lanino said. Many found it difficult to understand why they had experienced such violence. Lanino is concerned about the long-term impact of the conflict. "If these traumas are not addressed, they could seek revenge, because all this stress, all this trauma, could erupt in a new wave of violence." Sudan's army has launched a new offensive in Kordofan from the capital, Khartoum, and says it has taken control of the 360-kilometer-long highway linking Omdurman, Khartoum's twin city, with el-Obeid. SAF Chief of Staff Abdel-Fattah al-Burhan recently inspected the newly captured areas in North Kordofan by helicopter and congratulated his troops. The advance has reopened supply routes to SAF units in El Obeid. Residents of the previously besieged city celebrated the arrival of army forces, as the immediate threat appears to have receded for now. As they retreated, RSF fighters looted markets and villages in North Kordofan and committed human rights violations against local residents, according to the Sudan Tribune media platform. Last Monday, RSF commander Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as "Hemeti," told commanders in the affected areas they no longer needed to wait for orders from the high command and could instead launch counteroffensives at their own discretion. The move could lead to further attacks on civilians and additional looting. Who are Sudan's RSF? https://www.dw.com/en/spain-s-pm-visits-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5I40g Spanish authorities were overwhelmed by the latest influx Image: Atlas/REUTERS Advertisement Editors note: For more on the migrant crisis in Ceuta, Spain, follow our blog here . Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez , his interior minister and military personnel were bound for the North African enclave of Ceuta on Friday, a day after thousands of people gained irregular entry to the Spanish territory . At least 18 people died as tens of thousands of people rushed into the small Spanish coastal city, many of them drowning but some also perishing in a stampede to cross the breakwater fence. Authorities are still puzzling over what prompted such large crowds to suddenly seek entry. Regional government head estimates 60,000 new arrivals Preliminary estimates suggest that tens of thousands gained entry on Thursday alone as the Guardia Civil lost control of the border to Morocco . The head of the autonomous city governemnt, Juan Jesus Vivas, estimated that around 60,000 people had arrived, well over half Ceuta's population. "Estimates indicated that around 60,000 people have entered our city as a result of this event," he said. "This figure shows that it is impossible to absorb such pressure. It is absolutely impossible." Around 24 hours earlier, prior to the mass breach, Vivas had issued an esimate of between 1,500 and 2,000. Ceuta's population is roughly 85,000 people. "People are still entering. The reinforcements that have arrived are only helping the injured and other humanitarian efforts," Rachid Sbihi, who leads a local workers association representing Civil Guard officers, told the Associated Press. Both EFE and AP said correspondents observed some people seeking to return to Morocco on Friday, with the city's small migrant reception center completely overwhelmed. Border police said they had to switch their focus to trying to keep people safe, with at least 18 people killed in the chaos Image: Atlas/REUTERS Spain's PM Sanchez blames traffickers for misrepresenting court ruling Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez arrived in the territory on Friday along with Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska. In a press conference, he called the mass crossings a "violation of Spain's territorial integrity." Sanchez attributed the sudden increase in people seeking to swim around the border to a rumor being spread by human traffickers, deliberately misinterpreting a recent Supreme Court ruling. A Spanish Supreme Court ruled earlier in July that immediate returns of migrants crossing the border illegally did not apply to those arriving by sea. However, the case pertained to people crossing the Strait of Gibraltar or the Meditereannean Sea, not people swimming around a land border to enter Spain "by sea." "What has emerged from our talks with Moroccan authorities is that trafficking mafias took a self-serving interpretation of a Supreme Court ruling," Sanchez said. Those rumors "spread like wildfire in recent hours," Sanchez added, following the much slower start to the process earlier in the week before Thursday's rush . Spain has two enclaves, Ceuta and Mellila, on the North African coast bordering Morocco. A similar crisis hit Ceuta in 2021 , when more than 8,000 people are thought to have entered irregularly in a matter of days. Italy, Finnish minister question Spain's Schengen status Italy and France both announced they would temporarily boost border checks with Spain. "In response to the situation observed in the Ceuta enclave, I gave instructions as of last night to immediately strengthen the controls at the Spanish border. Furthermore, I am activating the Rapid Intervention Border Force for in-depth checks," French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez wrote online early on Friday. Italian right-wing Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni had on Thursday called for the "suspension" of Spain's Schengen membership. On Friday, Finland's Interior Minister, a member of the right-wing populist Finns Party that's the second-largest in Helsinki's coalition government, said she supported the proposal. "Spain has completely failed to protect the Schengen Area's external border from infiltration. This cannot continue. All European countries must support Meloni's proposal," Mari Rantanen wrote on Friday. Edited by: Darko Janjevic Don't let the algorithm hide the news. https://www.dw.com/en/spain-will-send-tr.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5I1Ze Video footage showed large crowds moving round the breakwater Image: Atlas/REUTERS Advertisement Officials in the Spanish territory of Ceuta on the northwestern tip of Africa on Thursday asked the government in Madrid to declare a national emergency and send the army to help secure its border with Morocco . The call came as video footage showed crowds of people trying to walk around the breakwaters separating Moroccan and Spanish territory or otherwise scale the border fence. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez pledged an "immediate response." Spain's Interior Ministry said later on Thursday that its armed forces would send personnel to Ceuta to support the border guards. "The Armed Forces will reinforce the Guardia Civil in the exercise of its powers and any others that may be necessary to maintain civil security in the city of Ceuta," the ministry said. What had happened in Ceuta during the day? The Guardia Civil said that crowds broke through the fences into Spain after overwhelming police at the city's breakwater. Video footage showed hundreds swimming across from the Moroccan side, using inflatable inner tubes and other flotation aids. "The situation is absolute chaos," Rachid Sbihi, head of the association that represents Spain's Guardia Civil in Ceuta, told the Associated Press. "It's not possible to give precise numbers but there are thousands of migrants crossing," he said, adding that the border had "totally collapsed." The AFP news agency cited a spokesperson for the Spanish government's delegation in Ceuta as saying that nine people had died amid the offshore rush. The scenes were reminiscent of a similar flashpoint at the border crossing in May of 2021 when more than 8,000 people entered the territory in just two days. In recent days, rescue parties had already noted increased numbers of people trying to swim around the border checks. An official from Spain's Guardia Civil policing the border described the situation as 'absolute chaos' Image: Atlas/REUTERS What did the regional government say? Juan Jesus Vivas, head of the Ceuta regional government, called for the Spanish government in Madrid to declare an emergency on grounds of national security, asking for more police and for the army to be deployed on the border. This followed a meeting of the city's board of spokespeople, who reached a unanimous agreement. "Yesterday, I spoke out to warn of the extreme gravity of the migration crisis we are enduring," Vivas wrote online. "Today, mere hours later, the situation is even more critical: another night of mass arrivals, nearly a thousand people waiting outside the CETI [Temporary Migrant Reception Center], our reseources completely overwhelmed, and another life lost at sea." The head of the regional government said its migrant reception center known as CETI had nearly a thousand people waiting outside. Here you see a much smaller crowd outside the facility on Sunday. [FILE: July 26, 2026.] Image: Antonio Sempere/JNA Press/Sipa USA/picture alliance He said that the small city was facing "a humanitarian and social emergency" of national proportions. "We cannot face this pressure alone — pressure that has resulted in the arrival of between 1,500 and 2,000 people in just 10 days, equivalent to 2% of our population." He wrote that "with every passing hour, the situation becomes more difficult" in the territory of around 85,000 people. How did Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez respond? Soon after the call for help from Ceuta, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said the government in Madrid was "fully committed to providing an immediate response" to the situation. "We are mobilizing all necessary resources, working with Moroccan and international authorities, and preparing the necesssary measures to restore normalcy as soon as possible," Sanchez wrote, adding that he had just said as much directly to Vivas. "This is the moment to build solutions, with responsibility and cooperation," he said, not going into specifics in the post. Sanchez's Interior Ministry said that the Moroccan government was "closely cooperating" with Spain to handle the situation and that Moroccan police were stopping "numerous people" trying to cross the border. It said that both countries had agreed to work together "for the return, as soon as possible, of all the people who entered Ceuta illegally." Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska made plans to visit Ceuta on Friday and evaluate the situation, the ministry said. Why is the rush happening now? It's not yet clear why large groups are suddenly seeking entry to Ceuta in the past few days, even though a couple of relatively recent developments at least bear a tangential relationship to the issue. Earlier in July, the Spanish Supreme Court ruled that migrants arriving by sea could not immediately be pushed back across a border in the same way as they could at a land border crossing. The Ceuta and Melilla enclaves in North Africa bordering Morocco do present exceptional cases where this ruling is concerned, in that it is technically possible to enter them "by sea" despite the fact that you are essentially circumventing a border crossing on land, not crossing the Strait of Gibraltar or the Mediterranean. One less recent development that attracted international attention, meanwhile, is the Spanish government's offer of amnesty and residency permits to migrants who can demonstrate that they had already entered the country without legal authorization. However, that rule only applies to people who can prove they were already in Spain when it came into force, so it does nothing to improve the prospects of staying for people entering by irregular means now. Italy's Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani, at least, drew a parallel between the amnesty and Thursday's events, calling for the EU's open-border Schengen area to be "closed to Spain," and alleging that the amnesty had encouraged human trafficking. Tajani's Spanish counterpart, Jose Luis Albares, condemned the Italian minister, saying it was "improper" for "a partner and friendly country from which we expect European solidarity and not partisan demagoguery." https://www.dw.com/en/how-two-wars-and-e.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5HoFl Supplies of rice — consumed by half the world's population — are at risk from El Nino Image: Amit Dave/REUTERS Advertisement A potentially record-strength El Nino is now intensifying across the Pacific, bringing either drought or flooding to the world's key farming regions. Earlier this month, the US National Oceanic & Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) predicted a 63% chance that the unusual weather pattern could be " very strong " this year. JP Morgan, meanwhile, warned last week that El Nino, combined with $100 (€88) oil prices, could spike food inflation by up to 1.5%. The arrival of El Nino follows two major conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East, during which global food supplies have held up remarkably well. So, could this third crisis bring the perfect storm that tips the balance? Are African nations underestimating the risks of El Nino? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Triple blow to global food security Russia's war in Ukraine still hangs over one of the world's major grain-exporting regions, where repeated attacks on ports and farmland continue to threaten one of the planet's key breadbaskets. The Iran war has driven up energy and fertilizer prices, raising the cost of growing food worldwide and causing temporary supply disruptions for key soil nutrients. El Nino, which shifts rainfall and temperature patterns worldwide, is expected to be so strong that the World Bank warned recently it could cut rice output by 20% to 50% in affected regions. Maximo Torero, chief economist of the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), warned of a "compound effect" that could create "a very complex situation" by the end of the year. "We are very concerned about El Nino and the delay of the monsoon ... in India ," Torero told DW. El Nino is expected to slow down and weaken India’s monsoon season , a vital time for rice planting. June already saw around 40% less rainfall than normal, according to local media. India produces nearly a third of the world’s rice, the vast majority of which is consumed domestically. Aside from South Asia, the FAO thinks the El Nino risks are highest in Africa's Sahel region , southern Africa , Southeast Asia and in the Dry Corridor of Central America. The UN food agency warned this month that some of these regions face a more than 50% chance of drought in the next few months. World producing more food than ever Despite the geopolitical strife, food prices remain nearly 20% below their 2022 peak, according to the FAO Food Price Index. The world brought in the biggest grain harvest in history last year. This is because farmers planted more land, the weather has been favorable and the crops produced more per acre. While this year is expected to be slightly smaller, the harvest will still be the second-largest ever. “We are seeing improvements in agricultural productivity," Simone Bunse, senior researcher at the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI), told DW, citing India and Latin America as notable examples. "These have helped sustain food production and reduce undernourishment. And this is balancing some of the localized impacts of conflict.” UN experts expect a 50% chance of drought across much of southern Africa Image: Jekesai Njikizana/AFP/Getty Images Millions still go hungry War is a major barrier to getting hunger under control globally. The UN says 266 million people are still facing acute hunger, more than half of them due to conflict. The worst of it is concentrated in just a handful of conflict-hit countries, including the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Sudan and Yemen, where supplies cannot reach the people who need them. "We have enough calories produced in the world to feed everybody," Torero said. "Those calories are not distributed in the same way across the world, and that's the challenge." War often destroys local food sources, displaces millions of people, damages infrastructure and severely cuts humanitarian access. In some hotspots such as Sudan and Gaza, experts say hunger is increasingly being used as a weapon. "Parties deliberately destroy farmland, livestock, water systems, food storage facilities, and transport routes. They jeopardize access to markets and obstruct humanitarian assistance," SIPRI's Bunse told DW. Farmers pinched by elevated fertilizer prices Another risk to global food supplies is fertilizer , around a third of which normally passes through the Strait of Hormuz . The strait remains heavily disrupted after a failed ceasefire between the US and Iran, along with attacks on shipping in the Red Sea . Some farmers have been paying substantially more for fertilizer, delaying purchases or switching to crops that require less fertiliser . If they ultimately apply less, yields could suffer in the next harvest. Food security experts believe the Middle East conflict alone could leave millions more people hungry by 2030 — and that projection does not yet account for the effects of El Nino. With temperatures in the Pacific Ocean expected to rise by 3.6 degrees Celsius (38.4 degrees Fahrenheit) — almost double the 2015/6 El Nino — climate think tank Berkeley Earth now predicts this year's weather pattern will be strongest on record. If oil prices leap past $120 a barrel again, if grain exports from Ukraine are successfully blocked, or if El Nino bites harder into next year’s crops as farmers plant less, then the world could face a spike in hunger, experts predict. If all of those happen at once, the impact would be far worse, with JP Morgan predicting that food inflation will surpass 5% in 2027 and that emerging markets would take the biggest hit. https://www.dw.com/en/the-slovak-village.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Hs7W Some residents of Vlkolinec would like their picturesque village's designation as a UNESCO World Heritage site to be revoked Image: Rob Cameron/DW Advertisement From the headlines in the world's media, the story seemed simple: A tiny Slovak village wanted UNESCO to remove it from the World Heritage List because of the pressures of overtourism . But that's not quite what is happening in Vlkolinec, central Slovakia . Interviews with residents, local officials and visitors suggest that the debate was less about UNESCO itself than about how to protect a living community from the pressures of tourism . Accelerated transformation "Those who come with humility, to admire the village and understand how people lived here, are always welcome," said 68-year-old Anton Sabucha. "They don't bother me. It's the rude ones." Sitting beneath an awning outside his wooden house, Sabucha leafed through a history of the village, pointing to photographs of neighbors and relatives. His wife brought out a tray of fried dough pastries. Vlkolinec in bygone days: Anton Sabucha says that the village's inscription on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1993 accelerated its transformation Image: Haris Jeelani Toogo/DW He remembered when around 200 people lived in Vlkolinec. Today, only 17 remain year-round. UNESCO did not create Vlkolinec's tourism problem. The village was designated a Folk Architecture Heritage Reserve in 1977, during the Communist era . But Sabucha argued that its inscription on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1993 accelerated the transformation, bringing visitors who too often forget that people still live in the centuries-old wooden houses. Diminishing privacy "You come out into your yard, wanting to sit quietly and have a coffee with your friends. Then the first tourist comes and asks, 'How are you? What's it like living here?' Then another. Then another," he told DW. Sabucha has erected a barrier at the entrance to his property bearing the notices "No Trespassing" and "No Photos." He said that despite this, some visitors still wander into private gardens, trampling flowers and treating the village as an attraction rather than a community. Vlkolinec resident Anton Sabucha says that some tourists often forget that people still live in the centuries-old wooden houses they come to admire Image: Haris Jeelani Toogo/DW "Someone sees the 'No Photos' sign and still has to take a picture. They simply don't respect people's privacy." Disappearance of traditional village life But the biggest loss, he said, has been the gradual disappearance of traditional village life. The surrounding meadows are no longer cut, the old agricultural terraces have become overgrown and many of the people whose lives have shaped the landscape are gone. Tourism income, he argued, has done little to reverse that decline. Residents receive around €400 ($455) a year from ticket revenues — "barely enough to buy a pallet of briquettes for the winter" — while many of those who now earn a living from tourism no longer live in the village, he said. "For an ordinary tourist, these are just wooden houses. For us, they're people. We know exactly who lived in each house." A living village Justine, a tourist visiting from France , said the village's appeal lay precisely in the fact that people still lived there. "Usually places like this are museums. Here, people still live here. That's unique," she told DW. When told that some residents wanted Vlkolinec removed from the UNESCO list because of tourism, she said she understood their frustration. Slovak village debates UNESCO status over tourism To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video "Having people walking around your village every day could become unpleasant," she said. "But at the same time, tourism also supports the region. It's difficult to know what's best." UNESCO status helps preservation Not everyone agrees that UNESCO is the problem. Miro Parobek, who oversees tourism for the town of Ruzomberok, which administers Vlkolinec as a municipal district, acknowledged that tourism had brought challenges. But he argued that the answer was better management, not removing the village from the World Heritage List. "Our first priority is to preserve the traditional architecture," Parobek told DW. "But our goal is also for this to remain a living village. We want to support the people who live here." He said the town had already responded to residents' concerns by replacing large festivals with smaller cultural events, while residents now met regularly with local officials through a dedicated working group. Miro Pirobek, head of Culture and Tourism in the nearby town of Ruzomberok, says that the priority is to preserve the traditional architecture of the village and support the people who live there Image: Haris Jeelani Toogo/DW The municipality also helped homeowners apply for grants to restore historical buildings and even provided twice-weekly transport into nearby Ruzomberok for older residents. Parobek said every entrance ticket carried the same message: "Vlkolinec is not an open-air museum. Please respect the privacy of the people who live here." Balancing tourism, heritage and residents' wishes He acknowledged that the balance between protecting residents and welcoming visitors was not always easy. Much of Parobek's optimism rested on plans that had yet to materialize. Ruzomberok was seeking Norwegian funding for a package of measures aimed at reducing pressure on the village, including a park-and-ride below the hillside settlement, improved footpaths and drainage, the restoration of traditional barns and terraces, and the conversion of the former village school into a community and cultural center. The project would also create more opportunities for local residents to work as guides and custodians, he said. Is removal from the list possible? Anton Sabucha is in a minority. But even if he somehow gets his wish, having Vlkolinec struck off the World Heritage List is an almost impossible task. It looks unlikely that Vlkolinec will become the first site to be removed from the UNESCO World Heritage List at the request of its residents Image: Rob Cameron/DW UNESCO has removed sites only three times since the program was established in 1978: Germany's Dresden Elbe Valley after the construction of a four-lane bridge , Liverpool's historical waterfront following large-scale redevelopment and Oman 's Arabian Oryx Sanctuary after most of the protected reserve was stripped of its status. In each case, UNESCO acted because the sites had irreversibly lost the qualities for which they had originally been inscribed. There is no precedent for a community asking to be removed voluntarily. And there is no sign that Vlkolinec is about to become the first to succeed in its request. https://www.dw.com/en/eu-civil-protectio.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Ht8H NASA satellites show the massive wildfire ravaging the Gironde region as France continues to battle raging wildfires Image: NASA/Bestimage/IMAGO Advertisement France is quite well-prepared for wildfires. The government operates 12 Canadair water bombers and eight Dash firefighting aircraft. In addition, leased aircraft and helicopters are being used. However, the fleet is currently needed simultaneously across many parts of the country. A drought has been intensifying for weeks, and several heat waves with temperatures sometimes exceeding 40 degrees Celsius (104 Fahrenheit) have left the vegetation extremely parched. The devastating wildfire near Bordeaux on the Atlantic coast has already engulfed more than 42,000 hectares of forest and vegetation. At the same time, fires and follow-up extinguishing efforts in southern and southeastern France are tying up additional emergency personnel. In many places, firefighters are battling the flames in an exhausting, round-the-clock effort. However, strong winds are fanning the fire fronts, making them almost unstoppable, and more than 220,000 people have had to leave their homes and vacation homes so far. The gravity of the situation is also underscored by the fact that the French government has deployed an A400M military transport aircraft equipped for aerial firefighting for the first time. The A400M can drop around 20 metric tons of fire retardant, more than three times as much as a Canadair. Nevertheless, the situation is currently so dire that President Emmanuel Macron also activated the EU civil protection mechanism (CPM) and requested assistance from other European countries. The French Air Force military transport A400M aircraft makes its first-ever drop of fire retardant Image: Abdul Saboor/AFP 24/7 service at the emergency response coordination centre To activate the CPM, a country reports its needs to the European Union's emergency response coordination centre, ERCC, in Brussels . ERCC experts assess which of the 37 participating countries can provide assistance. Initial assistance for France was mobilized within a few hours and has since been significantly expanded. Firefighting aircraft and helicopters from Portugal , Croatia , the Czech Republic , Germany , Turkey , Sweden and Slovakia are supporting France, primarily in the greater Bordeaux area. At the same time, however, the EU also dispatched six additional firefighting aircraft from Greece , Turkey and Italy to Spain . This means that 13 of the 22 firefighting aircraft available for this summer have already been mobilized for these two countries. The figures also demonstrate how quickly the European reserve can be drawn upon when multiple large-scale wildfires occur simultaneously. According to the European Commission , the resources currently available are therefore likely insufficient to keep pace with the scale of the fires . Turkey, Norway and others cooperate with EU members Since the launch of the civil protection mechanism in 2001, the system has been expanded several times. Since 2019, the EU has also launched rescEU, a strategic reserve comprising firefighting aircraft, medical equipment, field hospitals and specialized technology for chemical or nuclear emergencies. In addition to the 27 EU member states, 10 other countries are also participating in the civil protection mechanism, including Norway , Turkey and several Western Balkan states. For the summer of 2026, Brussels also pre-positioned 777 firefighters from 14 countries in particularly vulnerable regions of France, Spain, Portugal, Italy, Greece and Cyprus . The firefighting aircraft and helicopters of the European reserve are distributed across twelve countries and can be mobilized through the coordination center in Brussels. In addition, firefighting efforts are supported by high-resolution satellite imagery from the EU's Copernicus Earth observation program. The heart of this cooperation is that one country may be able to spare aircraft or emergency personnel while another urgently needs them. However, the European principle of solidarity reaches its limits in situations where multiple countries are simultaneously affected by extreme weather events , which are likely to occur with increasing frequency due to climate change. In such cases, governments must weigh how much support they can send abroad without jeopardizing their own operational capacity. Currently, Italy is battling wildfires within its own borders, even though it has not yet activated the mechanism. The European Commission expects an unusually long wildfire season this year. The mechanism was first activated at the end of April and could remain in effect until as late as early November. Even the sky glows deep red over Lake Moutchic as the Lege-Cap-Ferret wildfire illuminates the horizon in Gironde, France Image: Fabrice Sapte/ABACAPRESS/IMAGO Plans for a separate 'EU firefighting fleet' The current European air reserve for fighting wildfires consists primarily of nationally operated aircraft that are committed as EU resources for a specific period. Meanwhile, the EU is establishing a rescEU fleet — permanently available and fully funded by EU resources — at a cost of approximately €600 million ($682m). The plan is to acquire twelve new firefighting aircraft, which will be stationed in France, Spain, Portugal, Italy, Greece and Croatia. The aircraft will be operated by the respective member states, but decisions regarding their deployment within the rescEU framework will be made jointly by the European Commission and the participating countries. France owns several Canadair aircraft but needed to request help from abroad in fighting the current wildfires Image: Thomas Samson/AFP Wildfire prevention is key Europe's wildfire response force can save time in an emergency and relieve the strain on national disaster response teams. However, according to the European Commission, this cannot compensate for a lack of wildfire prevention measures such as the creation of firebreaks and stricter building regulations in high-risk areas. Furthermore, firefighting aircraft are most effective when fires are detected early. Once fire fronts measuring several kilometers have formed due to heat and strong winds, even additional aircraft from the European Union can often only contain the flames, but not fully extinguish them. Has Europe lost control of its wildfires? https://www.dw.com/en/poland-top-court-r.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5HtRT Poland's top court ruled the government's move to start recognizing same-sex marriages conducted elsewhere in the EU to be incompatible with the constitution [FILE: April 9, 2026] Image: Marek Antoni Iwańczuk/NurPhoto/picture alliance Advertisement Poland 's highest court, the Constitutional Tribunal on Tuesday overturned a law that would have led to the legal recognition of same-sex spouses who married in other EU member states and subsequently moved to Poland. The government in Warsaw had been moving to accommodate a ruling from the Court of Justice of the European Union saying that majority-Catholic Poland, which does not permit same-sex marriage domestically, must at least recognize unions contracted elsewhere in the EU . The unanimous ruling could set up a power struggle between Poland's top court and that of the 27-member bloc. What did Poland's Constitutional Tribunal rule? The court said in a statement on Tuesday that the judgment was unanimous and final and that EU same-sex marriages could not be copied into the country's civil registry as previously planned. It said that the plans for the "preparation and issuance of certified copies concerning unions contracted abroad that do not constitute a union between a woman and a man," were "inconsistent with Article 92, Paragraph 1, in conjunction with Article 18 of the Constitution of the Republic of Poland." Article 18 of the constitution reads as follows: "Marriage, being a union of a man and a woman, as well as the family, motherhood and parenthood, shall be placed under the protection and care of the Republic of Poland." In other words it both designates marriage as heterosexual in nature and as part of Poland's jurisdiction. Article 92, Paragraph 1 meanwhile states that regulations should be specified by "the organs specified in the Constitution." The court did not elaborate on its reasoning in its short statement, but this seemed to suggest its judges found that the European court order encroached on Poland's authority to set its family and marriage policies. Poland: Have things improved for the LGBTQ+ community? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video What had been previously agreed, when, and why? The November 2025 ruling from the Court of Justice of the European Union had not demanded that Poland legalize gay marriage, nor even that it recognize same-sex spouses as such legally. It did, however, demand that a same-sex couple who married legally elsewhere in the EU and then exercised "their freedom of movement to move and reside" in another state, like Poland, should have their marital status copied into the civil register if that was the only way to secure the benefits and securities of marital status in that country. The case was initiated by two men, a Polish national and a German-Polish dual national, who had married legally while living in Germany in 2018 and then moved to Poland the following year. Poland's Supreme Administrative Court had ruled in March that this step "does not violate national identity," nor interfere with Poland's authority to determine its own family and marriage laws. Poland's government subsequently implemented the legislation in May, and it had been set to come into force as of the end of August. But the right-wing opposition PiS party challenged the move at the Constitutional Tribunal, successfully as it transpires. Poland's Constitutional Tribunal and the top EU courts have clashed before, not least in a long-running dispute over the contentious appointment of new judges to the court when PiS was in government, with the most recent European Court of Justice rebuke of Poland's top court being issued last December . Poland, with roughly 70% of the population identifying as Roman Catholic in census data, is one of just four EU members not to permit either same-sex marriages or same-sex civil unions, along with Bulgaria, Romania and Slovakia. https://www.dw.com/en/as-us-iran-war-rag.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5HpPS Not as peaceful as it looks: During the US-Iran war the Strait of Hormuz has turned from shipping bottleneck to choke point. Image: REUTERS Advertisement The Strait of Hormuz has become one of the world's most dangerous waterways since March, when Iran began attacking shipping vessels as a pressure tactic in its ceasefire talks with the United States . Still, though a significant proportion of the global oil trade bottlenecks at the strait, shipping traffic never completely halted. With the United States and Iran issuing conflicting statements as to whether the Strait of Hormuz is open, DW analyzed public data sources to track how shipping traffic has changed during the course of the war and which vessels are still taking the risk of transiting the maritime choke point, which connects the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman. Shipping through Strait of Hormuz disrupted As Iran's strikes on and interception of vessels in the Strait of Hormuz continue, mines have also been reported in the prewar shipping lanes. The Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC), a project of the US-led Combined Maritime Forces, assesses the threat to shippers as "severe," its second-highest warning level. However, according to one of JMIC's latest advisory notes , issued after attacks resumed on July 6 and 7, "commercial traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remained at reduced levels, with vessels transiting via both the southern Omani corridor and the northern Iranian-controlled route." JMIC added that shippers remained cautious of transiting the strait amid the attacks on vessels in recent weeks. DW's analysis of data from the open-source platform Global Fishing Watch showed that, nevertheless, several shipping companies have navigated their vessels through the Strait of Hormuz throughout the war. Though the platform's primary purpose is to monitor fishing efforts, it also collects data on all other vessels using satellite imagery and relying on signals transmitted by ships' automatic identification systems (AIS). As ships can switch off their AIS transponders — and have reportedly repeatedly chosen to while transiting the Strait of Hormuz — the number of vessels is likely higher than shown. Based on AIS signals, a combined total of at least 84 ships crossed the Strait of Hormuz in two periods of the conflict: from the start of the war on February 28 until the announcement of a ceasefire on April 7 and following the renewed attacks on July 6 and 7. This aligns with reports of the United States saying it gave passage to about 70 ships and adding that not all of them transmitted signals. For comparison: In the same periods of 2025, more than 900 ships crossed the strait. Of these 84 ships, 34 moved from east to west into the Persian Gulf and 50 crossed the strait in the opposite direction, moving out of the gulf. In which countries are ships that transit the Strait of Hormuz registered? As part of the AIS signal, ships transmit which flag they are sailing under, but this information is entered manually aboard the vessels. In only a few cases investigated for this story did the flag reflect the actual country of origin of the registered owner or the ship manager of a vessel. This information can still be looked up manually in different databases using the ship's international ID number and its name. Only nine Iranian- and two Pakistani -owned ships transited under their respective national flags. All of the other 73 ships hoisted a flag different from the vessel owner's country. Analysis of this data shows that a wide variety of companies operating in the region continue to cross the Strait of Hormuz. At the top of the list is the United Arab Emirates , which neighbors the strait. The UAE's Abu Dhabi Crude Oil Pipeline (ADCOP) runs overland parallel to the waterway in the south. 13 cargo ships registered in the United Arab Emirates transited the strait during the shutdown, as well as two liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) tankers and three support vessels. Most of the UAE-based ship owners in the dataset appear to have only one to five vessels in their fleet. One of the UAE-registered vessels that was detected passing into the Persian Gulf on July 11 is managed by Lubeck Shipping LLC, a company associated with an Iranian oil tycoon that has been sanctioned by the United States . Also sanctioned by the United States is Salina Ship Management PvT Ltd. , a company from the Indian state of Maharashtra that US officials accuse of helping Iran move petrol. The company manages one of the four Indian oil and LPG tankers that Global Fishing Watch recorded transiting the strait. India , like many Asian countries, is heavily reliant on the Strait of Hormuz for energy supply. China , Pakistan and Vietnam , too, had oil and LPG tankers in the Persian Gulf that they moved out of the Strait of Hormuz before a ceasefire was announced on April 7. All seven vessels owned and managed by companies from Greece , the world's biggest shipping power, were freighters, typically carrying unpackaged dried goods such as iron, coal and grains. Why risk transiting the Strait of Hormuz? The primary motive for continuing to move oil and other goods via the Strait of Hormuz despite the threat of attacks by Iran is financial — "simply because the reward seems higher than the risk," said Matt Smith, director of commodity research at Kpler, a business intelligence company headquartered in Belgium that specializes in analyzing global commodity flows. "The key point is that producers of oil (or gas, aluminum, and other products) within the Strait of Hormuz essentially have only two options," economist David Wech wrote in an email. Wech monitors the flow of energy commodities such as oil and refined products for the British company Vortexa. "Option 1: to halt production and earn no money at all — or even incur losses due to operating expenditures," Wech wrote. "And option 2: accept the risk of transiting the strait and thereby earn 90% or more of their normal revenue. With an oil price of currently more than $80 per barrel, we're talking about billions of USD." With hostilities hot again as of July, the Brent Crude oil price is on yet another upward trend , perhaps one of the most perceivable global effects of the war and the near shutdown of the Strait of Hormuz. What are alternatives to Strait of Hormuz? In prewar times, roughly 25% of the global maritime oil trade passed through the Strait of Hormuz. Alternative routes have limited capacity to compensate for the loss of oil flow through the strait, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA). Two pipelines are currently used to bypass the Strait of Hormuz: the UAE's ADCOP and another in Saudi Arabia. The ADCOP in the United Arab Emirates would allow ships to land and load in the northeastern port of Fujairah and transport oil out of the Persian Gulf without transiting the Strait of Hormuz. The Abqaiq-Yanbu crude oil pipeline system (East-West Crude Pipeline or Petroline) in Saudi Arabia has some capacity left, the IEA reported in February. Publicly available shipping data for Yanbu show an increase in oil-related ship traffic from May through June, compared with previous years. "Combined, Yanbu and Fujairah have been able to reroute over 4 million barrels a day of crude from having to pass through the Strait of Hormuz," Smith said. "This has been able to act as a release valve to keep barrels flowing to key customers in Asia — but only offsetting 4 of the total 15 million barrels per day that typically passes through the strait." The alternative routes have their own risks. Reports are increasing of piracy and attacks on ships by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the narrow choke point between the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden. "Bab al-Mandeb has the potential to add further supply woes to a global supply picture that is already severely constrained," Smith said. So, the release valve to the Strait of Hormuz might soon become a maritime choke point of its own. Edited by Milan Gagnon and Andreas Becker. All data and code behind this story can be found in this Github repository . More data-driven stories by DW can be found here . https://www.politico.eu/article/ceuta-cr.text: Twenty-two EU leaders — including German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni — on Saturday took aim at Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez’s migration policies for undermining the security of the bloc’s borders. The increasingly isolated Sánchez hit back that his EU partners were responding in a “selfish” and “unlawful” manner to the sudden influx of some 50,000 unauthorized migrants from Morocco into the Spanish exclave of Ceuta in North Africa. While almost all those migrants have now returned to Morocco — and none crossed into the EU mainland — the 22 leaders raised “serious concern” over the threat to the EU’s frontier, and zeroed in on Sánchez’s move to grant legal status to up to 1.2 million unauthorized migrants as a “pull factor” that fueled the crisis. Advertisement Advertisement In a letter to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, European Council President António Costa and Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin, the 22 leaders made direct reference to the need for EU-level cooperation on policies such as Madrid’s migrant regularization scheme. “We have a duty to effectively deter and relentlessly combat illegal migration, by coordinating our action, strengthening our external borders and addressing all policies that can serve as pull factors, such as the regularization of [a] very large number of irregular migrants,” the leaders wrote. Madrid has pushed back against the claim that the country’s regularization scheme triggered the crisis in Ceuta, and has pointed out that none of the people who illegally entered the exclave would be eligible to benefit from the measure. “This process is based on very specific conditions, such as proof of residency in Spain before January 1, 2026, and having resided in Spain for five consecutive months at the time of application,” said a spokesperson for the Spanish foreign ministry. Moreover, the deadline for filing applications for the scheme, which was launched in April, was in June. But those explanations have not appeared to sway the EU leaders who signed the letter to Costa, Von der Leyen and Martin. “We cannot allow uncontrolled mass crossings, the instrumentalisation of migration or other hybrid threats to create the perception that illegal entry into the European Union is possible. That a migrant’s illegal entry can turn into legal stay,” they went on. Advertisement Advertisement In a sign of the increasing threat to the EU’s Schengen open travel area and the explosiveness of migration as a pan-European political issue, the letter’s signatories said they were ready to reinforce or reintroduce “temporary border controls” in the bloc. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez gives a press conference on July 28, 2026. | Javier Soriano/AFP via Getty Images In addition to Merz and Meloni, the letter was signed by the leaders of Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, Croatia, Cyprus, the Czech Republic, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Greece, Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, Malta, the Netherlands, Poland, Romania, Slovakia, Slovenia and Sweden. They called for a video conference of interior ministers to agree on next steps. Ireland said it would convene a meeting of the EU Justice and Home Affairs Council on Tuesday. Rome and Copenhagen took the initiative in drafting the letter. Sánchez slams ‘selfish’ counterparts In his own letter to von der Leyen, Costa and Martin, Sánchez slammed his European counterparts who “have chosen to attack Spain and to call for its temporary exclusion from the Schengen Area.” Italy’s Meloni on Thursday was the first to propose Spain be suspended from the 29-country zone where internal border controls have largely been abolished. Italy on Friday imposed restrictions on free movement from Spain to Italian ports and airports. France has also increased checks on the border with Spain because of the migration surge in Ceuta. Advertisement Advertisement In his letter, seen by POLITICO, Spain’s Socialist prime minister argued that calls to have Spain kicked out of the Schengen zone are “not only contrary to European law, humanitarian law, and the principles of solidarity that bind us together,” but also “Europe’s long-term interests and to the most basic common sense.” Sánchez defended himself from accusations that Spain was failing to protect the EU’s external borders, and cited data showing that his country had recorded half as many illegal entries as Italy between 2021 and 2026. He also stressed that it was not the first time that migrants had been weaponized against the bloc’s members, and recalled Belarus’ 2021 bid to sow chaos in the EU by facilitating migrant crossings into Poland and several Baltic countries . Spain’s prime minister added the EU members that had backed the suspension proposal were “driven by prejudice, fake news, ignorance, or political interest.” “In the current international context, the European Union cannot afford this kind of selfish, polarising and unlawful reaction,” he wrote. Sánchez’s strongly worded letter underscores the growing tension between the prime minister and the plethora of EU leaders that have expressed support for Spain’s temporary exclusion from the Schengen area. Those calling for action include right-wing politicians such as Finnish Interior Minister Mari Rantanen, a member of the nationalist Finns Party, as well as Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, whose Social Democrats belong to the center-left Party of European Socialists. Nicholas Vinocur, Zoya Sheftalovich and Sebastian Starcevic contributed reporting. Advertisement Advertisement

https://www.ibtimes.co.uk/andrew-tate-tr.text: The Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) has authorised a raft of new criminal charges against Andrew and Tristan Tate, including additional counts of rape, trafficking and sexual offences, bringing the total number of alleged victims in the UK case to seven.Andrew Tate, 39, has been charged with seven further counts of rape, three counts of arranging or facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation, three counts of assault occasioning actual bodily harm, and 19 additional offences relating to indecent images of a child and extreme pornography.His brother, Tristan Tate, 38, faces two further counts of rape, one count of sexual assault and three counts of arranging or facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation.The alleged offences are said to have taken place between July 2010 and August 2017.Brothers Arrested in US as UK Seeks ExtraditionThe brothers were arrested by the US Marshals Service in Miami on 18 July following an extradition request from UK authorities.The CPS said it is seeking their extradition to face both the original charges and the newly authorised offences.Malcolm McHaffie, Head of the CPS Special Crime Division, said the latest charging decisions followed a further file of evidence submitted by Bedfordshire Police.'We have decided to prosecute Andrew and Tristan Tate for further offences including rape, arranging or facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation and offences relating to indecent images of a child,' he said.McHaffie added that the additional charges increase the total number of alleged victims in the case to seven. He also urged the public to avoid commentary or sharing information online that could prejudice the ongoing proceedings.Total Charges Rise Against Both BrothersThe new charges bring the total number Andrew Tate faces in the UK to 42, including allegations of rape, human trafficking, assault and offences relating to indecent images of a child. Tristan Tate now faces 17 charges, including rape, sexual assault and trafficking-related offences.Bedfordshire Police said detectives from its major crime unit had worked closely with the CPS and law enforcement partners in the UK and overseas throughout the investigation.Assistant Chief Constable Karena Thomas said: 'There is no place for male violence against women and girls, and we will continue to work tirelessly to support victims and investigate all reports made to us.'Legal Battle ContinuesThe brothers are expected to appear before a federal court in Miami as extradition proceedings begin.Their lawyer, Joseph McBride, said they deny all allegations and argued the UK should not seek extradition while criminal proceedings in Romania remain ongoing.Andrew and Tristan Tate, who hold dual British and American citizenship, are also facing separate criminal proceedings in Romania over allegations of human trafficking and sexually exploiting women. The brothers deny all wrongdoing in both the UK and Romania.The Department of Justice confirmed the arrests were carried out by the US Marshals Service under existing extradition treaties between the United States and the United Kingdom.

https://english.news.cn/20260719/946d04a.text: Hungarian president signs constitutional amendment ending own mandate Source: Xinhua Editor: huaxia 2026-07-19 01:56:30 BUDAPEST, July 18 (Xinhua) -- Hungarian President Tamas Sulyok on Saturday signed the country's 17th constitutional amendment, triggering the end of his mandate as head of state. Once the law is published in the official gazette, the termination of his mandate will take effect the following day. In a video statement, Sulyok said he had signed the amendment because he had "no constitutional means of acting against this amendment, which violates constitutional principles but was adopted by the National Assembly (parliament) ... through a lawful procedure." Prime Minister Peter Magyar welcomed the signing, saying it had "removed the last obstacle to implementing our joint decisions." He said he would consult parliamentary parties on a successor, adding that "the moral basis of the nomination can only come from the trust of society." Sulyok was elected by Hungary's then Fidesz-majority parliament in 2024 for a five-year term, with his mandate originally due to expire in March 2029. However, Magyar has repeatedly called on Sulyok to resign, accusing him of serving the interests of the previous Fidesz government. The constitutional amendment ending Sulyok's mandate was adopted by parliament earlier this week after Magyar's ruling party secured the two-thirds majority needed to amend the constitution. Under the constitution, parliament must elect a new president by secret ballot within 30 days. Any Hungarian citizen aged 35 or older is eligible for the office if nominated by at least one-fifth of lawmakers, or 40 members of parliament. Until a new president takes office, presidential duties will be exercised by Speaker of Parliament Agnes Forsthoffer. The new head of state will assume office on the eighth day after the election result is officially announced. Magyar has said he wants to nominate a candidate capable of representing the unity of the nation and winning support from opposition lawmakers, although he has not yet named a candidate. He has also said the latest constitutional amendment is intended as a temporary arrangement and that Hungary will eventually introduce direct presidential elections under a new constitution to be approved by referendum. ■

https://english.radio.cz/july-1971-pragu.text: CS DE EN ES FR РУ УК July 1971: Prague city centre is declared historic preservation district Facebook Twitter Prague is known as one of the most beautiful cities in Europe. To preserve its unique character for future generations, its historic city centre was designated the Prague Heritage Reservation 55 years ago, on July 21, 1971. It covers a vast area of 895 hectares, making it one of the largest protected urban centers in the world. The district in question includes the Old Town, Malá Strana (the Lesser Quarter), Hradčany, New Town, Vyšehrad and large sections of the Vltava River with its islands. It is a place where medieval streets, Romanesque cellars, Gothic churches, Baroque palaces and modern architecture all come together. And all of this in a single vibrant city that was neither destroyed by war nor rebuilt after widespread demolition. In 1992, Prague’s historic centre was added to the UNESCO World Heritage List. The reason was simple: the city has a unique skyline, exceptionally rich architecture and an urban structure that has been preserved in an unusually authentic form. For visitors, downtown Prague is a romantic place steeped in history. For locals things are sometimes more complicated. About 45,000 people live in the historic district today, roughly half the number recorded in the 1980s. Many buildings have been converted into hotels or short-term accommodations, so everyday life is gradually disappearing from the area. Tourism is important for Prague, but it also brings problems: congested streets, noise, a lack of services for locals, and pressure for further construction. UNESCO has repeatedly warned of risks that could damage the historic skyline, such as high-rise buildings in Žižkov or Pankrác. In recent years, Prague has been working to improve the situation. The city has adopted a management plan for the UNESCO site and has begun to more strictly regulate construction in the areas surrounding the centre. The goal is a simple yet challenging task: to preserve Prague’s beauty while maintaining everyday life, rather than turning it into an open-air museum for tourists. REUTERS/Benoit Tessier July 17 (Reuters) - President Volodymyr Zelenskiy on Friday took steps to repair a rift with key ally Poland over his decision in May to name a ‌Ukrainian army unit in honour of World War Two fighters who killed Poles. Zelenskiy ‌chaired a meeting of senior officials devoted to relations with Poland and pledged to expand investigations into those killings ​by the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), a pro-independence armed group, and open intelligence files. Zelenskiy told the meeting that improved ties were critical in view of Poland's considerable help to Ukraine since Russia's invasion of its smaller neighbour in 2022. Polish President Karol Nawrocki stripped Zelenskiy of Poland's top honour ‌after he announced the naming plan. "We are ready for a serious and ​friendly ​dialogue on the issues that unite us and those ​that divide us today," Tusk wrote ‌on X. At the meeting, Zelenskiy pledged new diplomatic measures to ease tensions and said officials would open the archives of the Security Service of Ukraine and the Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine on mass killings of ethnic Polish civilians in the Volhynia region, now in northwestern Ukraine. Ukrainian officials have given no indication ​that they will rescind ​the decision to name the army unit after the UPA, saying it is up to Ukraine to decide which heroes it is to honour. https://www.ibtimes.co.uk/tate-brothers-.text: Just months after returning to the United States with vocal support from figures in Donald Trump's political circle, Andrew and Tristan Tate have been arrested by US Marshals on a British extradition request and now face dozens of criminal charges in the UK.The Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) has authorised a series of additional charges against the brothers, including new counts of rape, trafficking and sexual offences, bringing the total number of alleged victims in the UK case to seven.Andrew Tate, 39, has been charged with seven further counts of rape, three counts of arranging or facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation, three counts of assault occasioning actual bodily harm, and 19 further offences relating to indecent images of a child and extreme pornography.Tristan Tate, 38, faces two further counts of rape, one count of sexual assault and three counts of arranging or facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation. The alleged offences are said to have taken place between July 2010 and August 2017.From MAGA Backing to ArrestThe arrests mark a dramatic shift for the brothers, who were allowed to leave Romania earlier this year after spending more than two years under travel restrictions while facing separate criminal proceedings there.During that time, several high-profile figures aligned with Donald Trump publicly questioned the Romanian case. Donald Trump Jr described Andrew Tate's detention as 'absolute insanity', while Romanian Foreign Minister Emil Hurezeanu said a Trump administration envoy raised the brothers' case during the Munich Security Conference.Although there is no evidence the Trump administration secured their release, the Tate brothers' return to Florida fuelled speculation that they had gained influential supporters within Trump's political movement.That perception is now being tested after US Marshals arrested the brothers on behalf of UK authorities.UK Widens Criminal CaseThe latest charges bring the total number Andrew Tate faces in the UK to 42, including allegations of rape, human trafficking, assault and offences relating to indecent images of a child. Tristan Tate now faces 17 charges, including rape, sexual assault and trafficking-related offences.Malcolm McHaffie, Head of the CPS Special Crime Division, said the new charging decisions followed a further file of evidence from Bedfordshire Police and increased the number of alleged victims to seven.He also reminded the public that both defendants are entitled to a fair trial and urged people not to publish material that could prejudice the proceedings.Extradition Proceedings BeginThe brothers were arrested by the US Marshals Service in Miami on 18 July following the UK's extradition request. The Department of Justice confirmed the arrests were made under existing extradition treaties between the United States and the United Kingdom.The Tate brothers are expected to appear before a federal court in Miami as extradition proceedings begin.Their lawyer, Joseph McBride, said they deny all allegations and argued the UK should not seek extradition while separate criminal proceedings in Romania remain ongoing.Andrew and Tristan Tate, who hold dual British and American citizenship, also face criminal proceedings in Romania over allegations of human trafficking and sexually exploiting women. They deny all wrongdoing in both Romania and the UK.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwym.text: Image source, Reuters Image caption, Tristan and Andrew Tate pictured sitting together at a UFC match in April By Kathryn Armstrong Â and Â Claire Keenan Published 19 July 2026 Controversial influencer Andrew Tate and his brother Tristan have been arrested in the US after British authorities issued 38 new charges against the pair. The UK's Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) said Andrew was being charged with seven further counts of rape, as well as charges relating to sex trafficking and indecent images of a child. Tristan's charges include two counts of rape and three counts of arranging or facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation. The total number of charges against the brothers is now 59, police said. The alleged offending is said to have taken place between July 2010 and August 2017. The Tates have previously denied any wrongdoing. Following their arrest, prosecutors will begin legal proceeding to extradite the brothers, who are dual British-US citizens, to the UK, the CPS said. "These charging decisions followed receipt of a further file of evidence from Bedfordshire Police and bring the total number of alleged victims in this case to seven," Malcolm McHaffie, Head of the Special Crime Division at the CPS, said. Bedfordshire and Hertfordshire police have been investigating a number of offences in what it called a "complex investigation". As a result, 38 new charges were authorised against the brothers, meaning Andrew, 39, faces a total of 42 charges in the UK and Tristan, 37, faces 17. The US Marshals confirmed to the BBC that the Tates had been taken into custody, while a US Department of Justice spokesperson said the arrests were "pursuant to extradition proceedings". A lawyer who represents the Tates, Joseph McBride, said "the world knows Andrew and Tristan are innocent" in a statement released after their arrest on Saturday evening. "Their enemies know it best of all. That is exactly why they have been attacked," McBride continued, describing the new UK charges as a "political hit". He said the new charges were designed to counter a defamation action filed by the brothers in the US. "We are confident that once a competent judge sees the facts, and once the Department of Justice confronts this egregious abuse of its own authority, Andrew and Tristan Tate will walk free. America does not do Britain's political dirty work," he continued. Figure caption, British police issue 38 new charges against Andrew and Tristan Tate In 2024, Bedfordshire Police secured European arrest warrants for the pair to have them returned from Romania, where they are based and are under criminal investigation. In June, the brothers lost a legal bid to be told the names of their UK accusers , after the CPS decided it was necessary to withhold the names of their alleged victims until legal action formally started. Lawyer Matt Jury, who represents several alleged British victims of Andrew Tate, welcomed the charges and said: "Andrew and Tristan Tate are accused of some of the most serious offences, including multiple counts of rape and human trafficking. It is time they face justice". https://edition.cnn.com/2026/07/18/us/ta.text: US Marshals arrested social media influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate in Miami Saturday on an extradition request from the United Kingdom following an investigation into sexual offenses reported by seven victims, according to the UK Crown Prosecution Service. UK officials accused the brothers of abusing women in the East of England region, just north of London, between 2010 and 2017. Andrew Tate, a self-proclaimed misogynist with billions of views online, faces 42 charges, including rape, human trafficking, indecent images of a child and assault, according to the UK Crown Prosecution Service and Bedfordshire Police. Tristan Tate faces 17 charges, including sexual assault, rape and trafficking, officials said. “Officers from our major crime unit have been working closely alongside the Crown Prosecution Service and both national and international law enforcement agencies as part of this complex investigation,” Bedfordshire Assistant Chief Constable Karena Thomas said. The Department of Justice confirmed US Marshals arrested Andrew and Tristan Tate “pursuant to extradition proceedings,” adding the arrests “were made in accordance with the treaties and law enforcement agreements governing Justice Department extraditions.” The brothers will appear in Miami federal court on Monday, their attorney, Joeseph McBride, told CNN on Sunday. The brothers are expected to reject the extradition request, McBride added. The brothers are innocent, McBride said and criticized the UK’s move to seek extradition. “There is a long-standing agreement between the UK and Romanian governments that the UK would not seek extradition while the Romanian proceedings are pending,” McBride said. “Those proceedings are ongoing right now. That agreement exists because no nation gets to trample the judicial sovereignty of another for political convenience.” In a statement posted to X Sunday, McBride said the brothers were arrested for their politics and are being held in solitary confinement. The brothers were in Washington, DC, earlier this month where they held political meetings, McBride told CNN. CNN has reached out to Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier for information about where and how the brothers are being held. Romanian prosecutors previously accused the brothers of trafficking women across Romania, the United Kingdom and the US and sexually exploiting them. The Tates have repeatedly rejected the allegations made against them in that case. CNN has reached out to Romania’s justice ministry for comment on their arrest. Advocates have warned against the pair’s rising tide of influence among young boys and men. Andrew Tate is known for his aggressive speech about male dominance, female submission and wealth. At one point, he was suspended from major social media platforms. The brothers, who have dual American and British citizenship, face dozens of new charges added onto previous charges brought by the Crown Prosecution Service after evidence was submitted by Bedfordshire Police, authorities said. The new charges were brought after officials had investigated reports made by four additional victims in the East England areas of Bedfordshire and Hertfordshire, police said. Andrew Tate is also facing a civil suit in the UK, which is being brought by four women who accuse the social media influencer of rape. A spokesperson for Tate previously told CNN that their client “categorically denies these unproven and untested allegations.” Matthew Jury, an attorney representing the four women, welcomed Tate’s arrest. “We do not yet know whether these new charges relate to the complaints made by my clients or by other women,” Jury said in a statement Sunday. “But any step that advances the proper administration of justice deserves to be welcomed.” The brothers left Romania after Romanian authorities lifted travel restrictions on them, arriving in Florida in February 2025. Upon their arrival, they found themselves at the heart of another criminal investigation — when Attorney General Uthmeier announced the probe, led by the Office of Statewide Prosecution. They had taken aim at Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, who previously suggested they were not welcome in his state. “When Americans who are unfairly imprisoned abroad return home you betray them,” Andrew Tate said on X last year. “You better nail me now. Let’s go. Arrest me.” Thomas, the Bedfordshire Police official, said “there is no place for male violence against women and girls.” “We will continue to work tirelessly to support victims and investigate all reports made to us,” Thomas said. This story has been updated with additional information.

The US Marshals Service confirmed the arrests.The charges announced by British prosecutors significantly expand the case against the social media influencers, who have consistently denied all allegations.Officials said the warrant remains sealed. The precise legal basis filed in the United States has not yet been made public. A person familiar with the matter told The Guardian that the arrests were made following a UK extradition request.Also read: Why Andrew and his brother Tristan Tate were arrested in Miami? What we know so far New charges against Andrew, Tristan TateThe UK's Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) announced fresh charges against both brothers after receiving additional evidence from Bedfordshire Police.Andrew Tate, 39, now faces seven further rape charges, three counts of arranging or facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation, three counts of assault occasioning actual bodily harm, and 19 additional offences relating to indecent images of a child and extreme pornography. Prosecutors said the alleged offences occurred between July 2010 and August 2017.Tristan Tate, 38, faces one count of sexual assault, two counts of rape and three counts of arranging or facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation stemming from the same investigation. The CPS said the latest evidence increases the total number of alleged victims in the case to seven.The brothers already face a separate UK criminal case. Andrew Tate has been charged with 10 offences, including rape, human trafficking and controlling prostitution for gain involving three alleged victims. Tristan Tate faces 11 charges connected to one alleged victim. Both men have denied all wrongdoing.Also read: Fact check: Is Gov. Andy Beshear trying to fill Mitch McConnel Senate seat as he remains absent?Will the Tate brothers be extradited to the UK?The arrests do not automatically mean Andrew and Tristan Tate will be transferred to Britain.Under US law, a federal court must first determine whether the UK extradition request satisfies the requirements of the US-UK Extradition Treaty. The brothers will have the opportunity to challenge the request through the American court system. If the court certifies the extradition, the final decision generally rests with the US Secretary of State.The UK proceedings are also separate from the brothers' criminal case in Romania. Romanian prosecutors charged both men after their 2022 arrests with human trafficking, rape and forming an organized criminal group.Earlier this year, a UK High Court judge rejected the brothers' attempt to obtain the identities of the women accusing them in one of the British cases.
