GelÅ«nas / BNS Under a new proposal from Lithuania's presidential palace, migrant workers who have lived and worked in the country for two years would be legally required to leave for six months â a rule that not only risks forcing them away but could also block them from family reunification and from ever gaining permanent residency. The following is an opinion piece by Dr. Skirmantas Bikelis, Senior research fellow at Law Institute of Lithuanian Centre for Social Sciences. Skirmantas Bikelis | V. Raupelio / LRT nuotr. How well people of different backgrounds live together is a complicated question â as complicated as society itself. Trying to sum up migrant integration and social wellbeing with a single number or percentage is not just imprecise, it can be actively misleading. Yet that is exactly what is happening in Lithuania's current immigration debate, and foreigners living here should understand what is being proposed and why. Earlier this spring, Vilnius mayor Valdas Benkunskas made himself something of a laughing stock among experts by announcing a supposedly scientifically-proven figure. According to him, once migrants reach 10% of a city's population, this marks a "tipping point" leading to the formation of migrant ghettos â and he used this claim to argue for stricter, migrant-unfriendly measures in the capital of Lithuania, where migrants already make up that proportion of the population. Sociologist Karolis Å½ibas, founder of the NGO Diversity Development Group, dismissed this, saying that Benkunskas' "10% tipping point" argument was plucked out of thin air, with no research to back it up. In reality, according to Å½ibas, ghettos or segregated neighbourhoods form because of factors like lack of affordable housing, housing discrimination, income inequality, or gaps in education, not because of any specific percentage of foreigners. Still, these are problems worth fixing regardless of how many migrants live in a country. A new figure, this time from the presidential palace Now a new, even smaller number has emerged â this time from the office of President Gitanas NausÄda â being used to justify tightening immigration rules further. Foreigners currently make up 7.5% of Lithuania's population, and the president's chief adviser, Vaidas AugustinaviÄius, argues this figure already needs to be "managed" and "restricted." At the president's initiative, the National Security Group within the presidential palace has drafted amendments to the Law on the Legal Status of Aliens. If passed, these changes could make it significantly harder for many labour migrants to build a stable life in Lithuania â and could even push existing migrant workers to leave, with little incentive to come back. Vaidas AugustinaviÄius | J. StaceviÄiaus / LRT nuotr. What's being proposed? First, the president is proposing to change how labour migrant quotas are calculated so that they include not only newly arriving migrants but also those continuing to work in Lithuania. This would sharply reduce â essentially by half â the quota available for new arrivals, unless the overall quota were doubled. It is not clear if that's happening any time soon. Secondly, perhaps the single most consequential change in the package: labour migrants would be required to leave Lithuania for at least six months after every two years of work. A presidential adviser, Evelina GudzinskaitÄ, has defended this by suggesting it simply gives workers a natural chance to visit family back home, in line with how their work cycles operate anyway. But this framing misses the real impact. Migrant workers can already visit their families whenever they choose - they don't need a forced six-month 'deportation' to do so. Worse still, under current Lithuanian law, migrant workers only gain the right to bring their families to live with them after two continuous years of legal residence. So, a mandatory six-month departure every two years would permanently block that right, meaning workers could never reach the residency threshold needed to bring their spouses or children to Lithuania. It would also prevent them from ever qualifying for permanent residency, which requires five continuous years in the country, and eventually citizenship. Lithuanian passport | E. BlaÅ¾ys / LRT Why family reunification matters - and why blocking it backfires EU law on family reunification recognises that living together as a family supports social stability and helps migrants integrate into their host country, which in turn benefits the wider economy and society. When families live together, money spent on housing and living costs stays in Lithuania rather than being sent abroad. Research in criminology also suggests people with family responsibilities are generally more likely to follow the law (as per Robert J Sampson and John H Laub's theory of informal social control). Blocking migrants from settling permanently or reuniting with their families would strip away their motivation to learn Lithuanian, put down roots, or build a long-term future here. As Ivanas Trunovas, a migration researcher at Diversity Development Group, puts it: "There is a worrying trend in Lithuania â rules are being tightened for both those already living here and new arrivals. This reduces their motivation to integrate and build a long-term life in the country. If we don't see newly arrived people as part of our shared future, and don't guarantee them opportunities, protection and access to services, the result will be that Lithuanian residents of foreign origin become less willing to integrate." The justification The explanatory note behind the proposal argues Lithuania has reached its limit on accepting migrants, that the country has not invested enough in integration services, and that a more "flexible" labour market requires higher turnover of foreign workers. This reasoning does not hold up well. Once again, attempting to justify strict anti-immigration measures with a particular figure (7.5%) makes for a rather flimsy argument. After all, the principle of "no person, no problem" belongs to undemocratic regimes, not a welfare state. And if integration services are indeed lacking, the answer is to fund and build them â not to close the door on migrants Lithuania actually needs. Notably, these restrictions are aimed squarely at labour migrants who create very few problems: people invited by Lithuanian employers, who have income, housing, and background checks from the police and security services already in place. What they typically need isn't extensive economic support, but basic cultural integration help â such as accessible language courses. That should not be difficult to provide. Yet it is precisely these workers - the ones actively sought out and needed by Lithuanian businesses - who are being targeted. Lithuanian language (associative image) | J. StaceviÄiaus / LRT nuotr. Aurelija MaldutytÄ, president of the Lithuanian Confederation of Employers, has pointed out that Lithuania has faced a decade-long shortage of long-haul lorry drivers, welders and other specialists that local workers simply won't take on. Annual quotas for hiring foreign staff already run out before the year ends. Despite this, the presidential palace wants to make it harder to bring in exactly the labour migrants the country badly needs. What's really driving this? So, the presidential palace's proposal appears to be bad for Lithuania's economy, and works against the welfare of migrant families and their prospects for successful integration. What, then, is really driving such proposals? The need for labour market flexibility, cited by the presidential adviser, hardly sounds like a sufficiently weighty reason. A more revealing comment came from employers' representative MaldutytÄ in a radio discussion, when she said many Lithuanians feel uneasy about foreign workers - not because of anything they've done, but because of unfamiliar language, culture, or religion. That discomfort appears to be borne out in survey data: research from the Lithuanian Centre for Social Sciences and Diversity Development Group found that only around half of Lithuanians would support the country accepting labour migrants from outside the EU, and a similar share said they would not want Muslims living in their neighbourhood. Yet there is no evidence that migrant workers or Muslims living in Lithuania are causing any significant problems. The unease seems rooted less in facts than in unfamiliarity and fears stoked by some commentators and politicians - including false claims that migration is "out of control" or drives up crime. If policy continues to be shaped by these sentiments rather than actual scientific evidence, the risk is a set of rules that damage both Lithuania's economy and the wellbeing of the society it is meant to protect â including the migrant families already contributing to it. (AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson, Pool, File) (AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson, Pool, File) MIAMI (AP) — Social media influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate will fight extradition to the United Kingdom, where the brothers are accused of rape and sex trafficking, their lawyer said Monday, suggesting their arrest in Miami was politically motivated without explaining why. The Tates appeared in federal court Monday for the first time since their arrest on Saturday and are being held in federal detention. In the coming weeks, a U.S. district judge will consider whether they meet the conditions for extradition. U.S. Magistrate Lauren Louis set another hearing for July 27. In court documents unsealed Monday, U.S. prosecutors described allegations from the United Kingdom against the brothers involving three victims. One woman accused Tristan Tate of rape and assault during a long-term relationship with him beginning in 2012, including when she was unconscious, reporting him to U.K. authorities multiple times. Two other women, one who met Andrew Tate through a webcam business and another through a dating app, also accused him of rape and assault in 2014 and 2015. The brothers, through their social media empire promoting wealth, male dominance and misogyny, are among the world’s most polarizing internet personalities. Normally photographed in tailored suits and fitted shirts, they wore tan jail uniforms and handcuffs during Monday’s brief hearing. Neither brother said a word. Their attorney, Joseph McBride, insisted they should remain in the U.S. “We are of course objecting to extradition because Andrew and Tristan are innocent,” McBride said after the hearing. “They’ve never done nothing wrong. They shouldn’t be extradited for crimes they did not commit.” The brothers were surprised when they were arrested, McBride said, adding that the attempt to have them extradited was politically motivated. “There’s no question about it,” he told reporters. He suggested the Tates’ case “had a lot to do with” former British Prime Minister Keir Starmer’s decision to step down, without providing any details, and said it was no coincidence that the brothers were arrested after meeting “friends in Washington, D.C.” “We went to see our Congress people in D.C. and now we’re getting arrested. This feels political,” McBride said. He didn’t specify who the pair met with or what was discussed. On Sunday, McBride said he was confident the extradition request would be denied. Prosecutors in Britain said the new charges relate to four new victims and were brought after authorities received evidence from Bedfordshire Police in southeastern England. The allegations, spanning 2010 to 2017, include rape, assault, trafficking and offenses relating to “indecent images of a child and extreme pornography.” McBride said none of the latest accusers have been identified, adding “we’d like to know who’s accused Andrew and Tristan of what.” The brothers are already charged with rape, bodily harm, human trafficking and controlling prostitution for gain relating to three other alleged victims in the U.K. between 2012 and 2015. Their lawyer said in a statement Saturday that he believed the arrests were “greenlighted by a low-level functionary” at the Justice Department without input from leadership. The Justice Department told The Associated Press that the arrests were approved by leadership of its Criminal Division. The new allegations are the latest in a long-running international legal saga involving the Tates that has spanned the U.S., Britain and Romania. The brothers have repeatedly denied wrongdoing. The dual U.S. and British citizens moved to Romania in 2016. They were arrested there in 2022, accused of participating in schemes to lure women for sexual exploitation. They denied those allegations and the Romanian case hasn’t gone forward because of legal and procedural problems. Last year, they were allowed to leave Romania and flew to Florida. The former professional kickboxers have millions of followers on social media and are vocal supporters of President Donald Trump. Andrew Tate, 39, first became known a decade ago when he was a contestant on the U.K. reality television show “Big Brother.” He was booted from the show when a video appeared to show him assaulting a woman. He has amassed over 10 million followers on X but has been banned from other platforms for violating hate speech guidelines, including YouTube, TikTok and Instagram. He has made widely condemned comments, such as saying women who are sexually assaulted should bear some responsibility for the attacks and sharing graphic descriptions of how he might attack women. The Tate brothers have consistently denied allegations of abuse and human trafficking, claiming their violent and misogynistic statements have been taken out of context or were intended as jokes. ___ Associated Press reporters Alanna Durkin Richer in Washington and John Seewer in Toledo, Ohio, contributed. Source: Sándor Palota, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons Hungarian President Tamas Sulyok has signed a constitutional amendment that immediately ends his term in office, formalizing a major political overhaul led by Prime Minister Peter Magyar and his ruling Tisza party. The move marks another step in Magyar’s campaign to dismantle institutions established during former Prime Minister Viktor Orban’s 16-year rule. The constitutional amendment, approved by Hungary’s parliament, cites a “serious loss of confidence” in Sulyok, who was elected president in early 2024 with support from Orban’s nationalist Fidesz party. Although Sulyok approved the legislation, he said he did so because it complied with the legal process, while warning that the measure undermines Hungary’s constitutional democracy and the rule of law. In a public statement, the former Constitutional Court judge described the amendment as a turning point for the country, arguing that removing public officials in this manner creates a dangerous precedent. He said the decision weakens democratic values, including the separation of powers and constitutional safeguards. Former Prime Minister Viktor Orban also condemned the reform, claiming it demonstrated that political power could now be used against anyone. His comments come as Fidesz continues to struggle following its decisive election defeat in April, which ended the party’s long hold on power. Under the amendment, Parliament Speaker Agnes Forsthoffer will serve as Hungary’s interim president beginning Monday until lawmakers elect a new head of state or until a new constitution comes into force. Parliament, where the Tisza party holds a two-thirds majority, has the authority to appoint a replacement. The constitutional changes also introduce a 12-year term limit for lawmakers and establish a mandatory retirement age of 70 for Constitutional Court judges. The rule will require Constitutional Court President Peter Polt, a longtime Orban ally, to step down. Since taking office, Magyar has repeatedly urged Sulyok to resign, accusing him of failing to act as a neutral head of state and instead serving the interests of Orban’s former government. Magyar said the reforms are intended to restore democratic accountability, recover public assets, and ensure the Hungarian state serves its citizens rather than entrenched political interests. https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: A Senate inquiry into the Albanese government’s gambling laws has heard allegations that betting companies and casinos are providing big spending punters with drugs, free accommodation and escorts. Anti-gambling campaigner Tim Costello told Monday’s hearing he was preparing to give a character reference to a man being detained in Sydney’s Silverwater prison, who was allegedly targeted by promoters. The man is preparing to plead guilty to charges over theft of more than $12m, Costello said. Costello alleged to the hearing that gambling companies including TAB and Sportsbet offered the man drugs, escorts, and free accommodation. He was given free accommodation at Star Casino. He had to leave each week so they could technically say he wasn’t living there and come back the next morning. He was the TAB’s biggest customer in that time. They were giving him $50,000 bonus bets. He was also Sportsbet’s biggest customer. They were flying him to grand finals. They were offering him escorts, drugs

Photograph: Luke MacGregor/Reuters Mohamed Al Fayed At least five Mohamed Al Fayed abuse survivors confirmed as human-trafficking victims Decision comes after group of survivors claimed ex-Harrods owner’s associates must have helped facilitate his crimes Helena Horton Sun 2 Aug 2026 19.01 EDT Last modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 21.30 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google At least five victims of the former Harrods owner Mohamed Al Fayed have been confirmed by the Home Office as victims of human trafficking. A group of survivors of abuse by the deceased businessman had called for the Metropolitan police to make trafficking the main focus of its investigation, arguing that Fayed could not have committed his offences without a steady stream of women sent to him by associates. The women were victims of international and domestic trafficking, and one survivor told the Press Association (PA) they were recruited to a false role within Harrods . Two further victims were hired for a legitimate role and then selected from the shop floor for abuse. These cases stretch from the 1990s to the most recent, which took place after the 2010 sale of Harrods. Officers are looking into who may have facilitated Fayed’s crimes, in an investigation known as Operation Cornpoppy. Four people have been questioned to date, 21 months after the investigation opened. One survivor, known as Justine, told PA she felt “shellshocked” when she received the conclusive grounds decision in June that she had been a victim of modern slavery. She added: “But it’s a really significant thing, getting that decision, seeing it in writing that you were a victim of modern slavery and trafficking is very … it’s really shocking to read.” Another survivor, Isabella, who worked in the chair’s office at Harrods in 2001, told PA: “He couldn’t have done what he did without Harrods processing women to him and silencing them afterwards. It wasn’t just Harrods, obviously. It was any entity that Fayed owned or had control of. It was his yachts, his aviation business, the Ritz Paris, his properties all over France and Monaco. It went as far as the States and the UAE – anywhere that man touched.” More than 400 allegations of sexual misconduct have been made against Fayed for the period between 1977 and 2014 – including claims of rape, sexual assault, human trafficking, false imprisonment, drugging, physical violence and forced abortions. The Egyptian businessman died in 2023 aged 94, without facing any charges. A woman who said she was sexually assaulted by Fayed previously came forward to say she had been trafficked in Paris on his orders in 2008 before being sent to London to be sexually assaulted by him. Pelham Spong, 40, from South Carolina in the US, said Fayed, who owned the Ritz hotel in Paris, had forcibly kissed her and offered her a salary of € 65,000 a year if she slept with him. Victims have previously complained of how the Metropolitan police have handled the investigations into Fayed’s abuse. The Independent Office for Police Conduct is examining complaints about the force’s handling of allegations between 2018 and 2024. A Harrods spokesperson said: “Harrods supports all survivors in their pursuit of justice and continues to work closely with the Met police on its investigation”. https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: Woman stands in front of her grandparents' home, where she previously lived, after it was destroyed by a wildfire, in Spokane, Washington, on 2 August. Photograph: David Ryder/Reuters View image in fullscreen Woman stands in front of her grandparents' home, where she previously lived, after it was destroyed by a wildfire, in Spokane, Washington, on 2 August. Photograph: David Ryder/Reuters Washington state Eastern Washington fires destroy 600 structures and force 60,000 to evacuate Wildfires in and around Spokane have stretched ability of federal and local agencies to fight blazes Associated Press Sun 2 Aug 2026 19.33 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Wildfires in eastern Washington state forced the evacuation of 60,000 people in the Spokane area while destroying at least 600 homes, businesses and other structures, authorities said on Sunday. The fires in and around Spokane, the state’s second largest city, burned about 8.2 sq miles (about 21 sq km), but they were among dozens across the western US that stretched the ability of federal, state and local agencies to fight them. A total of about 390 sq miles have burned across the state, and some of the fires, including those in the Spokane area, have not been contained. Officials also said that the evacuees in Spokane included patients at its US Veterans Affairs hospital. Heatwave scorching western US ups risk of hazardous fire conditions Read more Video from the Spokane area showed buildings on fire, black smoke billowing up near neighborhoods, and the smoking ruins of homes, with only chimneys still standing. Several officials expressed concern that the area does not appear likely to get a break in coming days from the weather, which is expected to remain dry. “We are not out of danger,” Maria Cantwell, the US senator, said during a news conference with federal, state and local officials in Spokane. “The next couple of days will be challenging.” But Spokane was hardly the only place struggling to contain fires. Crews using bulldozers and helicopters continued for the 10th day to fight a fire that has burned nearly 525 sq miles (about 1,360 sq km) of grassland in western Idaho, and eastern Oregon. The area is home to cattle ranches, and authorities said the fire is threatening more than 600 homes and 800 other structures. The weather in the area was expected to remain sunny – and dry – well into the week, with temperatures rising to more than 90F (32C) on Wednesday. Officials say the fire was caused by lightning. View image in fullscreen A vehicle and structure are burned on N Skyline Dr due to a wildfire on 2 August in Spokane, Washington. Photograph: Young Kwak/AP The National Weather Service issued warnings about the air quality in eastern Washington, eastern Oregon, western and central Idaho and western Montana. It issued red flag fire warnings for parts of Utah and Montana and western Nebraska, and extreme heat warnings for the southern parts of Arizona, California and Nevada and northern Montana. While temperatures Sunday in Spokane were forecast to remain below 80F, wind gusts from 35mph (56 km/h) to 45mph had been expected by the afternoon, said Benjamin Cossel, the public information officer for the federal response team from California, called in on Saturday night to deal with the fires. “We have weather working against us, and we have terrain working against us,” Cossel said. There were three fires in the Spokane area: the Old Trails fire, the Fairview fire and the Meadowview fire, and the state issued air quality warnings. Bob Ferguson, the Washington governor, declared a state of emergency on Saturday, and the National Weather Service issued a “particularly dangerous situation” red flag alert for eastern Washington. Authorities in Spokane set up a shelter at the city’s main convention center. View image in fullscreen A vehicle drives by as smoke billows from the Old Trails fire as wildfires burn in Spokane, Washington, on 2 August. Photograph: David Ryder/Reuters Chris Jordan, the Spokane county commissioner, said relatives of his were in an area affected by the fires and that they don’t know if their home is still standing. He said he spoke with them as they were leaving. “They’re in their car and all they can see is smoke everywhere, and it was incredibly scary for so many people,” he said during the news conference. Heather Rosenstrater, the president and CEO of Avista Corp, the area’s electric and natural gas utility, said about 10,000 people were without power on Sunday, down from a peak of 30,000. Avista needs to repair two transmission lines, she said, so it’s possible that demand for electricity over the next few days could cause outages. Meanwhile, several larger fires continued to burn in less populated areas north-west of Spokane, including one about 80 miles from the city that has burned about 210 sq miles. Another fire in eastern Oregon, about 70 miles to the north-west in the Stinkingwater Mountains, has burned about 336 sq miles. “The whole northwest is heavily impacted right now,” said Keila Vizcarra, the spokesperson for the federal team from California handling what has been named the Big Grass fire in western Idaho and eastern Oregon. Photograph: ABC Affiliate Kivi/Reuters View image in fullscreen Emergency responders at the site of a fatal shooting incident in Twin Falls, Idaho, on 1 August in this still image obtained from a video. Photograph: ABC Affiliate Kivi/Reuters Idaho Suspect in Idaho restaurant shooting died of self-inflicted gunshot wound, police say Twin Falls police chief believes Chad Williams, 24, was alone in Saturday attack that killed three people Marina Dunbar Sun 2 Aug 2026 18.27 EDT Last modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 18.28 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Authorities say the man accused of opening fire at a fast-food restaurant in Idaho is dead from a self-inflicted gunshot wound, as investigators say quick action by an off-duty law enforcement officer and an armed bystander helped prevent even more bloodshed. Speaking on Sunday, Matthew Hicks, the Twin Falls police chief, said investigators are confident 24-year-old Chad Williams carried out Saturday’s attack alone. The shooting left three people dead and seven others injured at the recently opened restaurant in Twin Falls, a southern Idaho city of about 56,000 residents. Officials said on Sunday that two of the wounded have been treated and released from the hospital, three remain in stable condition and two are still in critical condition. According to Hicks, an off-duty state trooper and an armed citizen, whose names have not been released, returned fire, causing the suspect to move away from the restaurant. “We believe their actions helped drive the suspect away from the scene, preventing further casualties,” the chief said. “We want to take a moment and commend the actions of the off-duty officer and the citizen, and their heroic action to stop this incident.” Shooting at In-N-Out Burger restaurant in Idaho leaves three people dead Read more Detectives are continuing to investigate what led to the attack, Hicks said, adding that Williams’ family has been fully cooperating with investigators. The police chief also pushed back on false claims circulating online that incorrectly identified another individual as the gunman, stressing that the person had “no involvement in this incident whatsoever”. Meanwhile, the owner of the fast-food chain confirmed that one of those killed was an employee. “My heart is broken, my chest is heavy, my eyes burn from the tears I’ve shed. We lost one of our beautiful Associates tonight,” Lynsi Snyder, the In-N-Out owner, said in a statement released early on Sunday on social media. “In-N-Out will be mourning with the families and praying for them as they tread through a very painful season.” The FBI is asking anyone with photos or video from Saturday’s shooting to submit the material as investigators continue to piece together what happened. Police responding to the scene located the suspected gunman’s body near the restaurant, Josh Palmer, the Twin Falls public information officer, said on Saturday. Authorities were still notifying relatives of the victims on Saturday night, Palmer said. The violence erupted around 2pm at the newly opened restaurant, located in a busy shopping plaza where hundreds of people were nearby when gunfire broke out. The Twin Falls resident Haley Dodaro, 43, and her mother went to In-N-Out for lunch Saturday afternoon. While waiting in the drive-thru line, they saw people running across the road and workers bolting out of the restaurant. At first, Dodaro thought there might have been a fire, but then a man directing traffic in a reflective vest said there was a shooter. “So that’s when we knew there was a shooting. People were running out crying and screaming. It was very scary,” Dodaro said to the Associated Press. Photograph: Social media/Reuters View image in fullscreen Smoke rises after a Ukrainian drone attack on a Wildberries warehouse in Novosemeykino, in Russia’s south-western Samara region, on Sunday. Photograph: Social media/Reuters Russia-Ukraine war at a glance Ukraine Explainer Ukraine war briefing: Kyiv’s forces hit Wildberries again amid deadly trade of strikes with Russia Drone attack on warehouse of Russian retailer triggers fire as at least 14 killed in cross-border exchanges; EU force boards Russian ‘shadow fleet’ tanker. What we know on day 1,622 Guardian staff and agencies Sun 2 Aug 2026 21.01 EDT Last modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 21.24 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Ukrainian drone strikes killed at least nine people in Russia on Sunday, with targets again including retail giant Wildberries, while Russian attacks on Ukraine killed at least five , according to officials in both countries. Drones attacked a Wildberries warehouse in the Samara region, about 800km (500 ​miles) from Ukraine’s most advanced military positions, governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev ‌said. There were ‌no casualties and a fire triggered by the attack was being put out, he said. Ukrainian forces have attacked about a dozen Wildberries sites since 18 July in an attempt to disrupt the operations of the company, which is Russia’s largest online retailer and a linchpin of the consumer economy often described as the country’s version of Amazon. Three people were killed and two injured in a drone attack on the Udmurtia region of Russia , acting governor Olga Abramova said. In the border region of ⁠Belgorod, three people were killed and five injured in Ukrainian strikes, the local taskforce reported. A Ukrainian drone struck an area next to ⁠a playground, killing one child and injuring two, acting regional governorAlexander Shuvayev said. Russian strikes in Ukraine killed two people in the eastern region of Dnipropetrovsk, and at least one person each in the southern regions of Zaporizhzhia and Kherson, according to regional authorities. A separate Russian strike destroyed a postal terminal in the northern Kharkiv region, killing a worker, the mail operator Nova Poshta said. View image in fullscreen A police officer at the site of the Russian guided bomb attack on a residential area in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine. Photograph: Daryna Naumova/EPA A strike on a Russian residential building in Samara’s neighbouring region of Saratov killed two people in the city of Engels , governor Roman Busargin ‌said. Civil infrastructure was damaged in Engels and the city of Saratov, he said. Ukraine’s military said on Sunday that their forces attacked the Saratov oil refinery and the Engels military airbase, sparking fires at both facilities. It said its forces also struck an oil depot in the western Kaluga region. Russia’s defence ​ministry said its forces struck infrastructure and two vessels with military cargo in the Ukrainian port of Mykolaiv, as well as a vessel carrying military supplies in the Black Sea. An EU naval mission led by Italy boarded a tanker from Russia’s so-called “shadow fleet” on Sunday, the ⁠second such operation in ⁠less than ​two weeks as Europe intensifies scrutiny of vessels suspected of helping Moscow circumvent oil sanctions. Italy’s defence ministry said the Toa Payoh, a ⁠tanker subject to EU sanctions, was intercepted west of the Sicilian island of Pantelleria while sailing from Benin to Istanbul. The vessel had switched to ⁠a Cameroon registry only last week, a source familiar with the operation said. "Officers of the Directorate for Combating Organized Crime have solved the homicide of a 38-year-old UK national, whose body was found inside a suitcase in an abandoned building in the Kypseli area on July 18," the Hellenic Police said on Sunday. Police say suspect confessed The victim, identified in British and Greek media reports as 38-year-old Elisabeth-Jane Ross from Scotland, arrived in Greece in late June and was last known to be in the Athens area on July 10. She was later reported missing. Police said the suspect, a foreign national, confessed on Thursday and now faces charges including intentional homicide, robbery and firearms-related offenses. "It emerged that the [suspect] placed the body in a suitcase and transported it to the abandoned premises. Furthermore, in the days that followed, the 26-year-old used the victim's bank cards to withdraw sums of money," police said. According to reports, the suspect said the victim was already dead when he found her, although police made no mention of this in their statement. A replica pistol and a knife were recovered from the suspect's home. Greek police said international cooperation, including support from Interpol authorities in the US and UK law enforcement agencies, helped identify the victim despite advanced decomposition. https://www.dw.com/en/pakistan-suicide-b.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5I9tq Hundreds of people protesting increased militant violence were present when the attacker detonated his suicide vest Image: Sherin Zada/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement A suicide bomber killed 14 people and injured dozens more in an attack targeting anti-militancy demonstrators in the city of Kabal in Pakistan 's northwestern Swat Valley. Five police officers were among those killed at the event, which was staged outside a local police station to protest growing militant violence in the region and the state's inability to protect citizens. Those gathered accused authorities of failing to act decisively against militants , saying residents want to live without fear after years of devastating violence. The area was the home of Nobel laureate Malala Yousafzai , who was shot there by a Taliban gunman in 2012. Hundreds of people were at the rally and social media video footage showed a speaker mid-sentence when an explosion rocked the area and sparked panic among demonstrators. "The suicide bomber blew himself up when asked for a search in front of the police station," a local police official said. No group has claimed responsibility for the crime. A former Taliban stronghold President Asif Ali Zardari and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif both condemned the attack. "Terrorists," said Zardari, "will never succeed in their nefarious efforts to harm peace, national unity and the writ of the state." Pakistan has experienced a surge in militant attacks of late, with many targeting police and security forces. The Swat Valley was a Taliban stronghold between 2007 and 2009, when Pakistan's military drove the Islamists out and re-established government control over the area. The religious militants have recently resurfaced, however, with the Pakistani Taliban , known as Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan, or TTP, being particularly active. The TTP is separate from, but allied with, Afghanistan's Taliban rulers and has been a source of tension between the neighboring countries. Pakistan says the TTP and other militant groups are carrying out attacks in the country with the support of Afghanistan's Taliban rulers and has promised to continue targeting the TTP and its support network. https://www.politico.eu/article/nigel-fa.text: LONDON — Over the past decade, Nigel Farage has ripped political conventions apart, dictated the debate on Brexit and immigration, and driven his party into contention to win the next general election. But now the hard-right Reform UK leader faces what may be the biggest challenge in a career suddenly engulfed by troubles. From a far more potent rival in new Prime Minister Andy Burnham to a resurgent Tory party, pressure over his finances, and a dubious gamble on a special election, Farage and his team are feeling the heat. And their poll ratings have started to slide. Advertisement Advertisement “Farage is facing something of a perfect storm,” said Tim Bale, professor of politics at Queen Mary University of London and an expert on the right in Britain. “But while he’s on the ropes he’s by no means on the floor, let alone out for the count.” Farage insists he won’t be “cowed” by what he describes as intimidation and says he is preparing for a general election as soon as this autumn, although Burnham has said he has no imminent plans to call one. It’s an open question whether the Burnham bounce in the polls and the dip in Farage’s fortunes mark a decisive shift in momentum in British politics or merely a blip. What is clear is that the challenges facing Reform are substantial, and growing. Farage’s side admits that Burnham has lifted the Labour government since he took office on July 20 and hurt Reform with a blizzard of policy pledges and energetic social media videos that have dominated media attention. Reform’s leader, meanwhile, has been beset by questions over whether he broke parliamentary rules by not declaring a £5 million donation. Last month he quit parliament to trigger a special election in his constituency of Clacton on the east coast of England, vowing to take on the establishment he says is trying to stitch him up over the furor. But with none of the mainstream parties willing to play ball, the contest has assumed an air of farce: Farage’s only well-known opponent is a candidate who goes by Count Binface, a serial joker who dresses up as a trash can. Advertisement Advertisement As if that weren’t damaging enough, the Conservative Party that Farage has spent much of his career tormenting is staging its own recovery in the polls, as leader Kemi Badenoch strengthens her position. Even the number of migrants arriving in small boats has fallen, robbing Reform of its signature attack line to use against the government. The result is a notable slide in the polls both for the party and for Farage himself. Polling pains According to POLITICO’s polling partners, London-based Public First, Farage’s net approval rating has dropped from -16 in early May to -21 at the end of July. Among people who voted Conservative in 2024 — a key target group for Reform — his rating has fallen by 15 points over the same period. “Reform has lost significant support among the people who historically voted Conservative since the local elections,” said Seb Wride, head of polling at Public First. “Rather than being able to get on the front foot during the early weeks of Burnham’s leadership, the Clacton by-election is making Reform seem less relevant, and Labour has been able to largely ignore them while defining what they stand for under new leadership.” In a slew of headline voting-intention polls in recent days, Burnham’s Labour has pulled level with Reform and in some cases taken the lead, ending 15 months of consistent national poll leads for Farage’s party. Andy Burnham walks near the White Cliffs of Dover in England during a visit to HM Coastguard Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre on Aug. 2, 2026. | Jack Taylor/ AFP via Getty Images “We have been here before. We have dealt with difficult moments before,” said Gawain Towler, a board member of Reform UK and the party’s former communications chief. The attacks on Farage over his financial arrangements are unfair, and come from questionable sources, he said, though they have caused damage even so. Advertisement Advertisement “There has been an impact and the Burnham bounce does also have an impact on the polls of course. The two things are happening together,” Towler said. “But what’s interesting is the impact these attacks are having on our supporters is very little because they expect the establishment to behave like this.” The great establishment stitch-up Public First’s analysis suggests there is truth to the idea that Farage’s core support has solidified as a result of his recent difficulties: During the same period that his overall approval rating has fallen nationally, from early May to the end of July, it has risen by 13 points among people who voted Reform at the last election in 2024. According to Towler, there is evidence that “the Establishment” is going after Reform with a series of underhanded leaks and attacks. That narrative — of a vengeful elite intent on punishing the people’s champion and the underdog — has proven powerful for populist leaders such as Farage, Donald Trump, Marine Le Pen in France and many others. Like Farage, however, Burnham is portraying himself as an outsider who is on the side of ordinary voters against the elite. The next election, whenever it comes, may be decided by which of these two can best embody the insurgent spirit. “Nigel Farage is the most scrutinized politician in British politics and he has been for quite a long time — because of what he represents,” Towler said. “He is the leader of a political party, one that threatens not just the political establishment but the establishment across the board.” Towler argued that the British establishment is trying to shake Reform’s confidence and soften it up for an election campaign, likening the assault to the prelude to the World War I Battle of Messines, with “heavy artillery for weeks and weeks, trying to break morale.” Advertisement Advertisement “If they manage to take Farage out, there’s a general election tomorrow. That’s what they’re trying to do,” he said. “They’re trying to break our morale as a party and I think you’ll find we have more morale, and we’re made of sterner stuff than they suppose.” Walking away Queen Mary’s Bale said that while Farage is in difficulty, his situation is “serious but not terminal — not yet anyway.” If polls worsen and the financial scandals deepen significantly, that could change, he said. “If he decides to throw in the towel — and given his record and his thin skin, nobody should rule out that possibility — Reform is in serious trouble.” Farage has history of walking away. He quit as leader of his previous party, the UK Independence Party, after losing his bid to win a parliamentary seat in 2015, only to be persuaded to return a few days later. He also stood down as Reform leader and announced he would be retiring from politics in 2021, but jumped back into campaigning when former PM Rishi Sunak called a general election in 2024. That comeback decision, according to Towler, was the moment Farage reconciled himself to the hard reality of challenging the political establishment to win power. “He knew it was going to be really hard. He knew that not just him, but a lot of other people around him — his friends, his long-term friends and allies and supporters — are also getting attacked,” Towler said. “And this will continue. We know it will continue. But we then say, hold on, this is our country. We can’t give up. How can we possibly give up?” Advertisement Advertisement

https://www.politico.eu/article/greece-f.text: ATHENS — As Spain and France began to gain control over devastating wildfires that last week sparked one of their largest peacetime evacuations, Greece was battling multiple blazes on Sunday — and a sense that its odyssey is far from over. Two firefighters, a Greek and a Danish national, died after a pair of helicopters battling a major wildfire burning out of control west of Athens crashed in midair. Another Greek and a British national were recovered alive. Television footage showed one of the helicopters exploding and plunging to the ground in flames after the collision. Foreign firefighting and helicopter crews are often deployed in Greece to help tackle wildfires. Advertisement Advertisement Another three Greek firefighters died last Wednesday while tackling wildfires in Crete and on the Peloponnese, a rugged peninsula in southern Greece. While a fire that has been burning since Friday around Porto Germeno on the Gulf of Corinth some 60 ​kilometers northwest of Athens has subsided, on Saturday the flames crossed a mountain to the south, fanned by strong winds of up to 130 kilometers per hour, and reached the settlement of Veniza closer to the capital. According to initial estimates, the fire has destroyed around 200 houses in the area. On Sunday flames spread rapidly through western Attica, a region that encompasses Athens, threatening communities and an industrial district outside Megara, about 30 kilometers from the capital. Speaking on state TV Ert, the president of the firefighters’ federation, Nikos Lavranos, described it as a “huge front” and a “black blanket covering an area of around [25 acres].” Dozens of settlements have been evacuated, and firefighters are focusing on preventing the flames from advancing toward Megara, pop. 30,000. Greece’s firefighting service said more than 2,500 people had been evacuated in western Attica by late Sunday afternoon. “Unfortunately, we have uncontrolled fires in far too many areas. As soon as the fire brigade arrives at one spot, just as the fire is being brought under control, it flares up again in another spot,” Megara Mayor Panagiotis Margetis told Open TV. Firefighters were also fighting another blaze in the Peloponnese on Sunday as well as on the island of Cephalonia in the Ionian Sea between Greece and Italy. More than 500 firefighters have been deployed across Greece. Advertisement Advertisement Wind speeds are set to drop significantly on Monday, according to the National Meteorological Service, which should ease the work of the fire services. Europe has been ravaged by wildfires this summer after months of record-breaking heat and little rain. Scientists have found that climate change vastly increased the likelihood of Western Europe’s record-breaking heat wave in late June as well as a spring drought — both events that made the land more fire-prone. Wildfires in France and Spain forced the evacuation of over 300,000 people last month. Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis expressed his “deepest sorrow” for the “tragic accident” of the helicopters, and pledged state support for those whose homes were destroyed. “There are moments when the force of nature and the intensity of weather conditions exceed all human planning and every operational capability,” he said in a social media post on Sunday. “These are extremely difficult days for our country.”

https://telex.hu/belfold/2026/08/02/laza.text: Menü Kereső Lázár János tavaly beismerte, hogy nem készült fel az Orbán-kormány a súlyos vízhiányra Belföld Nyilas Gergely Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! https://www.fenlandcitizen.co.uk/news/to.text: Home News Article Top Fenland Citizen stories include man hospitalised overseas, opening of Fenland’s first luxury cat hotel, and rapist to be deported By Molly Nicholas - Molly.Nicholas@iliffepublishing.co.uk Published: 06:00, 20 July 2026 Our biggest stories have featured a man hospitalised overseas, the opening of Fenland’s first luxury cat hotel, and a rapist to be deported. Meanwhile, an arsonist was jailed. Here are the biggest stories from last week across Fenland… GoFundMe page set up to help March man Danny Hayes who is fighting for life in Spain Danny is currently fighting for his life in hospital A fundraising page has been set up to support the family of a man who is fighting for his life in a hospital overseas. Danny Hayes, from March, remains in a medically-induced coma in Spain, currently “fighting for his life”, but his loved ones face high costs. After receiving “hundreds and hundreds of messages from people asking how they can help”, the family decided to start a GoFundMe page, which launched on Wednesday and has so far raised more than £6,460 of the £10,000 target, which will help fund the recovery of Mr Hayes. Part of Weasenham Lane in Wisbech closed while Anglian Water makes burst water main top priority The road has been closed while repair works are undertaken. Picture: Molly Nicholas A water company behind a hosepipe ban affecting the whole of Fenland has announced it is making a major water leak its priority. On Monday, one person took to social media with a video showing water spouting out of Weasenham Lane in Wisbech – outside of Wilco Motor Spares – with water building up and lying across the road. This area has become a hot spot for burst water mains and sinkholes in the past, with many long repair works taking place. Longcroft Luxury Cat Hotel opens new venue in Upwell Deputy mayor Vivienne Spikings (centre) cut the ribbon, alongside founding director Abi Purser (centre left) and owner Nichola Hannigan (centre right) A luxury cat hotel is up and running, ready to welcome pets to experience its “five-star boarding experience”. Longcroft Luxury Cat Hotel Upwell celebrated its grand opening last Sunday, greeting guests to Fenland’s first-of-its-kind premises. Deputy mayor Vivienne Spikings officiated the ribbon-cutting ceremony alongside hotel owners and family team Nichola Hannigan, her husband Andrew and mother Elaine. They were joined by Longcroft Luxury Cat Hotel founder Abi Purser. Arsonist jailed for setting light to number of vehicles in Chatteris and Wisbech Rolandas Fedoren has now been jailed. Picture: Cambs Police A man who set fire to numerous cars across Fenland has been jailed for more than a year. Rolandas Fedorenko, 25, torched a Nissan Juke in Furrowfields car park, Chatteris, in the early hours of April 1 last year. He lit a toilet roll and plastic and put it under the bumper, leaving the vehicle to burn out and damaging a nearby van and fence in the process. Then, later in the year, he began starting fires again. Former Wisbech mayor and rapist Aigars Balsevic to be deported when released from prison Aigars Balsevics, the former mayor of Wisbech, was convicted of rape in 2023 A former mayor who is serving time for rape has lost his legal battle to avoid deportation. Aigars Balsevics, 45, who made history as a town’s first mayor from Eastern Europe after taking on the role in Wisbech in 2020, has had his human rights appeal rejected by an Upper Tribunal judge following a long legal challenge. The Latvian national, who is serving a six-and-a-half-year sentence after being convicted of two counts of rape at Peterborough Crown Court in 2023, had argued deportation would affect his relationship with his two children – a son and daughter born in 2015 and 2017. Wisbech mum launches own Slimming World group after amazing weight loss Rosie after she lost four stone A woman who transformed her health, confidence and lifestyle with a weight loss group is now preparing to help others do the same. Rosie Harpum, a mum of one, knows first-hand how difficult managing weight can be while balancing the demands of family life. Having previously been a Slimming World member before becoming pregnant with her daughter, Rosie had enjoyed success with her weight loss journey. However, like many parents, her focus naturally shifted to caring for her family, and her own health gradually took a back seat. Human Interest Molly Nicholas MOST READ

https://udaipurkiran.com/president-murmu.text: Chisinau, July 20: President Droupadi Murmu arrived in Chisinau on Monday, marking the first visit by an Indian president to Moldova as part of her tour that also includes North Macedonia and Romania. She was warmly welcomed at Chisinau International Airport by Moldova’s Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Mihai Popsoi. The President’s secretariat shared the news on social media platform X, stating, “President Droupadi Murmu has arrived in Chisinau, Moldova, as part of her state visit to Moldova, North Macedonia, and Romania. Upon arrival at Chisinau International Airport, she was warmly welcomed by the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Moldova, Mihai Popsoi. This is the first visit by an Indian president to Moldova.” President Murmu is visiting Moldova at the invitation of President Maia Sandu. During her visit, she will engage in discussions with President Sandu and meet with Igor Grosu, the President of the Moldovan Parliament. According to the Ministry of External Affairs, she will also interact with members of the Moldova-India Parliamentary Friendship Group and address a business forum along with members of the Indian community. The Ministry stated, “India and Moldova share good and friendly relations. This visit will prove to be a significant and historic milestone, elevating the relationship between the two countries to a major partnership. There is ample scope for mutually beneficial cooperation in agriculture, health facilities, pharmaceuticals, IT, and education.” On July 17, during a special briefing on President Murmu’s visit to Moldova, Secretary (West) of the Ministry of External Affairs, Sibi George, mentioned that the visit would provide an opportunity to review the relations between the two countries and discuss ways to enhance cooperation. He noted that President Murmu’s visit would help strengthen business-to-business linkages and promote trade and investment relations. Sibi George added, “This visit offers a chance to review the entire spectrum of relations between the two countries and discuss ways to enhance cooperation, advancing the relationship with political goodwill towards significant partnerships in areas such as trade and investment, digital technology, innovation, renewable energy, health facilities, education, agriculture, culture, and connectivity.” The Moldova leg is the first stop on President Murmu’s three-country tour, after which she will head to North Macedonia and Romania for high-level meetings. The company, Greece’s main domestic manufacturer of weapons systems and ammunition for the armed forces, is targeting revenue of 40 million euros in 2026, up from 14.08 million euros in 2025. It also expects to return to marginal profitability after posting a net loss of 2.2 million euros in 2025, compared with a loss of 25.01 million euros in 2024. HDS reported a positive gross profit of 11.8 million euros in 2025, reflecting improved production performance. Shareholders’ equity and working capital also turned positive for the first time since the company’s establishment. Outstanding loans stood at 73.1 million euros as of Dec. 31, 2025. New strategy aims for financial self-sufficiency According to sources, HDS’s management has prepared a new strategic and business plan, which is expected to be presented at an extraordinary general meeting scheduled for late July 2026. The plan aims to make the company financially self-sufficient within the next three years, eliminating the need for recurring state financial support. The previous business plan was drafted about 15 years ago. https://cphpost.dk/2026-07-20/opinion/wh.text: The EU Pay Transparency Directive has been introduced to close gender pay gaps and enhance transparency in compensation practices across EU member states. It applies to public and private-sector employers, requires specific reporting obligations, and will significantly impact employee benefits and total renumeration analysis. At its core, the Directive does two things: it gives employees the right to know what they can expect to be paid and how that figure was reached, and it requires employers to account for their pay decisions with data. This is a shift from pay being a private, discretionary decision to pay being a governed, defensible one. The headline from the 7 June 2026 deadline, when the Directive should have been implemented locally, is that four member states have fully transposed the EU Pay Transparency Directive, and twenty-three have not. With the deadline extended to 1 January 2027, I can understand why this is being read as a reprieve. It would be reasonable to conclude you have time if you are watching this from outside the countries that have legislated. But, in my opinion, I’d argue the opposite is true — and I want to explain why. As it stands, the mandatory gender pay gap reporting deadline of 7 June 2027 remains the same. This is based on full-year 2026 data and there is no extension for organizations to review their existing pay structures, introduce new procedures, and implement reporting systems. Regardless of when each member state transposes the Directive into domestic law before the new deadline of 1 January 2027. This is also a moment of visible disruption in talent management, and that is an opening. It’s the opportunity at which pay equity work can be positioned inside broader business strategies related to restructuring and workforce planning, rather than treated as a compliance function afterwards. HR, Talent Management, and Total Rewards leaders who use this window to build the business case, should find it easier to secure the budget, support, and mandate this work requires than those who wait until a domestic deadline forces the conversation. The Directive Doesn’t Change. What varies across the transposition process is procedural: timelines, enforcement mechanics, the precise wording of definitions, and the size of administrative fines. What doesn’t vary is the substance. Every member state is transposing the same core obligations, including salary range disclosure at the point of hire, the right to information on pay levels, mandatory gap reporting above defined thresholds, joint pay assessments where unjustified gaps exceed 5%. It is also worth remembering that Denmark, Cyprus, Estonia, France, Ireland, Latvia, Poland, Romania and the Netherlands have already published draft legislation. While Germany, Spain, Greece, Finland and Czechia are working through theirs. Only Sweden has formally paused its process. Where it gets interesting is what happened in Romania in June. In the space of twelve days, members of parliament registered the transposition bill with the Senate under emergency procedure, the Legislative Council issued their formal recommendations and concerns, and the bill was reassigned an official legislative number and sent to committee with a 45-day deadline. The Legislative Council’s feedback did not question the obligations and whether Romania would require salary range disclosure, or workers would gain a right to pay information. It only concerned definitional precision, missing impact assessments, and the length of the remediation window. Even so, the EU Pay Transparency Directive can still be enacted in Romanian law by October 2026. It’s realistic to expect that the full transposition to take time, but Romania is an example of how quickly procedural systems can move forwards. What This Means for the Work You Should Be Doing Now. The fundamentals of pay transparency compliance are operational. Can you produce a defensible salary range for every open role? Can you explain, with data, why two people doing comparable work are paid differently — and is that explanation one you’d be comfortable giving to the employee directly, not just to a regulator? Do you have a job evaluation framework that classifies roles on the basis of skill, effort, responsibility and working conditions, rather than on legacy banding that nobody has re-examined in years? None of that work depends on your country’s transposition status. All of it takes months to build properly, and none of it can be assembled convincingly in the weeks before an enforcement deadline. Organizations that wait for their national legislation to be finalized before starting are choosing to compress twelve months of foundational work into whatever window remains before their country’s deadline. With increasing pressure from the European Commission and based on what has happened, that may arrive faster than expected. The Question Worth Asking Internally. Not, “Has our country transposed the EU Pay Transparency Directive yet?” The more useful question is: if it had, would we be ready? For most organizations right now, the honest answer is no. And the time to get ready is closing at the pace you set, not the pace your parliament sets. In my opinion, there really is no time to waste. Start the work now and fine-tune for when transposition happens within the next six months. Romanian Business News - ACTMedia :: Services | About us | Contact | RSS Home Daily Financial & banking Economic Companies Energy & Environment Almost half of fraud cases reported in the first half of 2026 were phone scams (vishing) ING Bank Romania, together with the National Directorate for Cyber Security (DNSC), the Romanian Police, and the Romanian Institute for Active Aging, organized ING SAFE Talks, a new event dedicated to informing the public about the latest methods of digital fraud. For the first time, telephone scams rank first among all types of fraud. Of the total incidents reported by the DNSC in the first half of the year, 42% were telephone scams (vishing), 14% were phishing scams, and 13% were SMS scams (smishing). Nationwide, in the first half of 2026, all criminal investigation units within the Romanian Police (which have jurisdiction over the investigation of cybercrimes and crimes against computer systems) recorded approximately 15,000 criminal cases. At the end of June, approximately 72,000 cases remained pending nationwide. As of January 1, 2026, there were 67,000 cases on record, according to representatives of the Criminal Investigations Directorate of the Romanian Police. ING Bank, DNSC, and the Romanian Institute for Active Aging are calling for increased vigilance against digital fraud During the ING SAFE Talks event, participants discussed the latest digital fraud schemes, how Romanians over 50 and seniors react to fraud, and new features from the ING SAFE ecosystem dedicated to fraud prevention were launched. “The methods used by attackers aren’t necessarily new, but the technology they use has evolved significantly, including through the use of artificial intelligence tools. At the same time, they are becoming increasingly skilled at social engineering techniques, which they use to convince people to provide them with data, send them money, or install malicious applications. As users, we must continue to be vigilant about three elements that we can identify in every fraud attempt – emotion, urgency, followed by a request for data. Initiatives such as today’s, in which ING, the DNSC, the Romanian Police, civil society, and the Romanian media come together to discuss the latest scenarios and stories used in fraud attempts, are essential – prevention remains just as important as responding to cyberattacks.” – Mihai Rotariu, Manager of the Communications, Marketing, and Media Division, National Directorate for Cybersecurity (DNSC). More than 6 in 10 Romanians aged 50 and older identify spoofing or bank impersonation as the most common method of fraud During the ING SAFE Talks event, the first national study on online financial fraud among people over 50 was also released. More than 6 in 10 people over the age of 50 say they have experienced at least one type of cyber fraud, while only 37% say they have never faced such a situation. On average, older adults are familiar with 7 of the 13 types of fraud analyzed in the study. According to the study*, Romanians over the age of 50 are familiar, on average, with 7 of the 13 types of fraud analyzed in the national study: 66% of respondents say they have heard of fake messages or calls that appear to come from a bank or other institutions (spoofing and impersonation methods), which is the most widely recognized fraud method analyzed in the study. Phishing – that is, sending suspicious links to fake websites that mimic official platforms—ranks second (63%), followed closely by offers for products or services at unrealistically low prices and messages or emails requesting passwords, personal information, or account updates (61%). More than half of respondents say they have heard of requests for money received via WhatsApp, Facebook, or TikTok (57%), as well as fake investments and unrealistic financial promises (56%). “The results of this study confirm that financial and digital education must become an ongoing process, adapted to the evolving nature of online fraud. Through the ‘Nesupus Fraudelor’ campaign, carried out in partnership with ING Bank Romania, we aim to provide seniors with practical information, concrete examples, and tools to help them recognize fraud attempts and respond appropriately. The study provides us with a clear picture of the challenges faced by people over 50 and will serve as the foundation for the next stages of the campaign.” — Alexandra Dobre, founder of the Romanian Institute for Active Aging According to the study, most people over 50 choose to take action when faced with a fraud attempt. Nearly seven in ten respondents (69%) say they contacted the police or other authorities, and 47% blocked the contact from whom they received the message. At the same time, more than one-third (36%) verified the information before taking action, and one in five (19%) chose to ignore the message. Only 11% of respondents admit to clicking on the link they received, and a similar percentage contacted their bank to verify the information. Online fraud has become a global, well-organized, and highly adaptable industry “We’re no longer talking about isolated hackers, but about organized groups with structures similar to those of companies: call centers, recruitment, and IT developers. Using artificial intelligence, fraudsters create voice and video deepfakes, as well as flawlessly crafted messages. Furthermore, personalization based on public data increases the attack’s credibility. The emotions most frequently exploited are: fear, urgency, trust, and financial gain.” — Alin Becheanu, Head of Fraud Monitoring & Prevention, ING Bank Romania At the ING SAFE Talks event, ING Bank Romania launched the ING SAFE ecosystem, which brings together the bank’s initiatives dedicated to fraud prevention and customer protection, as well as new security features. ING SAFE Call is a new security service designed to protect customers against attempts at financial fraud. When ING Bank’s monitoring systems identify a payment that deviates from the customer’s usual behavior, the customer automatically receives a verification call from the dedicated number 0374647233 (i.e., 037INGSAFE). During the call, ING Bank customers can confirm or reject the transaction: press 9 if they recognize and confirm the payment, or press 1 if they do not recognize the transaction or were tricked into making it. With the new ING SAFE Button feature, customers will be able to block access to their accounts directly from Home’Bank if they suspect fraud. Protecting customers from financial fraud is an ongoing priority for ING Bank Romania. We are constantly investing in both prevention and monitoring technologies, as well as in the development of new features that help customers identify and avoid fraud attempts before they can take effect. With the launch of the ING SAFE ecosystem, we are bringing all these initiatives together into an integrated approach that combines technological innovation, education, and partnerships with the authorities,” said Alin Becheanu, Head of Fraud Monitoring & Prevention at ING Bank Romania. How can we protect ourselves from online fraud? Be wary if you receive alarming messages or emails that try to convince you to take immediate action: “Your reservation will be canceled in 24 hours,” “Your account will be suspended.” Never click on links or open attachments from unknown sources if the message is unexpected or if you suspect something is wrong. Contact the platform’s team through a different communication channel to verify the message’s authenticity. Do not install apps at the request of supposed investment agents that would give them control over your device, whether it’s a cell phone or a computer. Warning: they will then have full access to your bank accounts and personal data and will be able to perform any transaction they wish! If you need help with a transaction, contact your bank Make sure you’re not on a clone site, which looks similar to the official one but uses a different or misspelled domain name (a missing or extra letter can be a clue). Never log in to your online banking app using a link received via text message or email, and don’t click on promoted links. Use only the app installed on your phone, or type the app’s URL into a new web browser window. Be wary of online offers that seem “too good to be true.” If they contain phrases such as “guaranteed-return investments” or “unbeatable returns,” they most likely come from scammers. Never complete a transaction until you’re sure it’s what you want. Carefully read any text messages you receive from your bank and make sure to confirm the transaction you intended to make. To recognize online fraud attempts and avoid falling victim to them, stay informed by checking reliable sources such as the DNSC website and the security section on the ING Bank website. To recognize attempts at online fraud and avoid falling victim to them, ING Bank Romania consistently ad vises banking customers to stay informed about these issues through reliable sources such as the DNSC website and the security section on the ING Bank website. Read our Privacy notice An English YouTube star who became famous playing Minecraft online will be extradited to Poland to face allegations of child sex crimes. Stuart Kluz-Burton, who is known online as Stuu, posts gaming , lifestyle and comedy-based videos. He has 4.1 million followers on YouTube and 1.8 million on Instagram. The London-born influencer , 34, is alleged to have abused minors in Poland. He faces two charges of sexual activity with girls aged under 15 and two charges of inducing minors to drink alcohol. He was initially ordered for extradition by a judge in February 2025, but appealed the ruling. Last week, the High Court upheld the original order, ruling that he will be sent to Poland. open image in gallery Stuart Kluz-Burton posts gaming and lifestyle content ( Supplied by Champion News ) Setting out the background in a joint judgment, Lord Justice Holgate and Mr Justice Johnson said that Kluz-Burton was born in the UK and holds dual British-Polish citizenship. He spent most of his life in Britain, before moving to Poland in 2014 and beginning his YouTube career. He became well-known online firstly under the name “Polish Penguin” and then “Stuu”. Through his various channels, which initially focused on videos about the popular video game Minecraft, he gained millions of viewers. His fame eventually lead to roles in the Polish language dubbing of blockbuster The Emoji Movie. However, he withdrew from his online activity, moving back to the UK support his Luton-based mother, who has cancer. Accusations about him began circulating online around 2023, as part part of what the judges described as a “wider scandal” in Poland known as “Pandora Gate”. The allegations of sexual activity with girls under 15 relate to an alleged incident in the summer of 2015 with one complainant, and another in August 2018. The alleged offences of inducing a minor to drink alcohol are said to have taken place in August 2018, involving two girls, including the alleged victim of the second sex crime. According to the Polish arrest warrant, the maximum penalty for the offences is 12 years' imprisonment. Kluz-Burton was arrested at his home in October 2023 and, after a hearing at Westminster Magistrates' Court, his extradition was approved by a judge. open image in gallery Kluz-Burton’s extradition was approved by a judge at Westminster Magistrates’ Court (file photo) ( PA Archive ) However, he challenged the decision, arguing that there was evidence that the Polish judge who initially signed the warrant was potentially under political pressure. On the same day that the allegations were brought to the attention of the Polish prosecutor, then-Polish prime minister Mateusz Morawiecki had published a video statement about the wider scandal. In it, he said: “We heard the story of a man who used his fame achieved on the internet to harm minors… These are behaviours of deviants and we will do our best to eradicate it as efficiently as possible... I ordered appropriate services to deal with it and I am expecting quick actions in this subject.” Kluz-Burton’s arrest by Interpol, the global network which connects police forces across the world, came only 10 days later, the day before the parliamentary elections in Poland. Recounting Kluz-Burton's arguments, the judges said his barrister Joel Smith KC had argued that the case cannot be treated as an ordinary request arising from ordinary allegations because the circumstances show there was “real political significance” at the time of the decision of the Polish judge who signed the warrant, Judge Lubowski. “The prosecution was initiated and accelerated in the days immediately preceding a national election, senior executive figures made repeated public statements about the allegations and demanded quick action on bringing a prosecution,” Kluz-Burton's lawyers had argued. It meant that the extradition arrest warrant was not issued by a “judicial authority” for the purpose of the Extradition Act 2003, they complained. But dismissing his appeal, the High Court judges said: “The fact is that this is a routine criminal investigation as opposed to an investigation that is inherently political. “It has achieved a high profile because of the nature of the allegations, their appearance on social media and Mr Kluz-Burton’s fame. “For those reasons it entered social media discourse. That high profile, and the publicity that was given to the allegations and the investigation, meant that there was a need for the court to act quickly. “The allegations emerged shortly before political elections. Politicians sought to make political capital out of them, but by making statements that were directed at the public, the police and prosecutors, not the court. “Viewed cumulatively, it has not been shown on appeal that the (magistrates court) judge’s conclusion was wrong, and that he ought to have found that Judge Lubowski may not have been independent and impartial. “The judge engaged with each of the arguments in support of the proposition that there was the potential for political interference. “He recognised that the statements made by senior politicians were 'a real matter of concern' and a 'striking feature' and that they were made in the context of a highly contested election. “He nevertheless concluded...that, taken at their highest, they were directed to the investigation and prosecution of the allegations rather than to the court, and that they 'did not amount to any form of pressure on the court to act in a particular way', thus embracing the risk of influence test. “Mr Smith says that conclusion is irrational. We disagree. The judge was entitled to reach that conclusion for the reasons he gave. “Nothing in the statements was explicitly or implicitly directed to any judge or court. None of them contained any implicit threat to take disciplinary action against any judge or risk of such action. “Some of the statements explicitly recognised that Mr Kluz-Burton’s guilt or innocence was yet to be determined and none of them sought to pre-judge that issue.” They said that the arguments did not “provide a basis for suggesting any lack of independence in this case” and rejected Kluz-Burton's appeal. Subscribe now > Rafaela Sousa 20 July 2026 Manufacturing Nestlé to cease production at Hungary confectionery plant Nestlé will cease production at its Diósgyőr, Hungary, confectionery plant in December 2026, citing declining demand for seasonal chocolate products. The company informed employee representative bodies of the decision this month. The facility currently produces hollow chocolate figures for distribution across several international markets. According to a Nestlé spokesperson, output at the plant has "decreased significantly" in recent years amid weaker demand for seasonal confectionery. The facility represents less than 3% of Nestlé revenue in Hungary and approximately 0.4% of its domestic production volume. Alongside preparations to halt production, Nestlé has entered advanced negotiations over the sale and future operation of the factory. The company said it hopes to transfer the facility to an investor that will continue confectionery manufacturing, potentially preserving employment for as many workers as possible. Nestlé said it will provide further information on the outcome of the advanced negotiations at a later date. The company’s hollow chocolate figures will remain available following the shutdown, with production set to move to an independent manufacturer operating in accordance with Nestlé’s quality standards. Nestlé added that its other Hungarian factories in Szerencs and Bük will continue operating and developing.
